guides.title: Adjusting Pole Length for Terrain
guides.summary: How to set and change trekking pole length for flat ground, climbs, descents, sidehills, snow, and stream crossings: the baseline elbow fit, how much to shorten or lengthen, choke-down technique, strap use, lock types, and pole care.
guides.safetyNote: Poles assist balance; they do not make dangerous terrain safe. Keep your hands out of pole straps during stream crossings, scrambles on rock, and travel in avalanche terrain or dense timber, because a trapped pole can wrench your arm or hold you under water. Never trust your full body weight to a single planted pole on steep ground, check that adjustable locks are tight before every descent, and treat swift or thigh-deep water as a serious hazard regardless of how good your poles are.

sections.heading: Why Pole Length Matters: What Poles Actually Do for a Moving Body
sections.body:
Trekking poles turn a walker from a two-legged creature into something closer to a four-legged one, and the benefits are measurable rather than mystical. With poles, a hiker has two extra contact points with the ground, which widens the base of support and dramatically improves balance on uneven footing, loose rock, mud, wet roots, and snow. On descents, poles let the arms absorb a share of the braking forces that otherwise pass entirely through the knees; biomechanics studies of steep downhill walking have measured meaningful reductions in the forces and torques at the knee joint when poles are used well, with commonly cited findings in the range of a 12 to 25 percent reduction in joint loading depending on slope, load, and technique. On climbs, poles recruit the arms, shoulders, and back to contribute propulsion, spreading the work of raising body weight across more muscle mass. Carrying a heavy pack magnifies every one of these effects, which is why backpackers adopted poles decades before day hikers did.

All of those benefits depend on geometry, and geometry is what pole length controls. A pole works best when it meets the ground at an angle and position that let the arm push through a strong, comfortable range of motion, roughly, forearm near level, elbow bent around a right angle at the moment of plant, with the push finishing behind the hip. Terrain changes that geometry constantly. Walk uphill and the ground rises to meet the pole tip, effectively making the pole longer than it was on the flat; the hands ride up, the elbows pinch closed, and the arms lose their pushing range. Walk downhill and the ground falls away, effectively shortening the pole; the hiker stoops forward to reach the ground, which loads the toes, cramps the diaphragm, and puts the body in exactly the pitched-forward posture that makes a slip worse. Adjusting length is simply the act of restoring good geometry as the ground tilts.

The cost of ignoring this is not just lost efficiency. Poles set too long for a descent force the hands high and the weight back on the heels late, or, more commonly, poles left too short for a descent pull the torso forward over the feet, and a forward-pitched hiker on steep loose ground has pre-loaded the fall that poles were supposed to prevent. Poles too long on a climb turn every plant into a shoulder shrug, and over a thousand meters of ascent that shrug becomes genuine neck and trapezius pain. Poles at the wrong length also encourage bad plant positions, tips flicking at the ground far ahead or trailing uselessly behind, which wastes the balance benefit entirely.

This guide treats pole length as a live variable rather than a number chosen once in a shop. The skills are few and quickly learned: establishing a correct baseline length for your height; knowing the standard corrections for sustained climbs, descents, and sidehills; using the grip itself, choking up and down, for terrain that changes too fast to justify stopping; setting straps and locks so the equipment transmits force instead of absorbing it; and knowing the situations, deep water, real scrambling, avalanche terrain, where the right adjustment is to get your hands out of the straps or put the poles away altogether. None of it is complicated, and all of it together is the difference between poles as decoration and poles as equipment.

sections.heading: The Baseline Fit: Sizing Poles for Flat Ground
sections.body:
Every terrain adjustment in this guide is measured from one reference setting, so establish the reference carefully. The standard baseline fit is this: stand on flat ground in the footwear you will hike in, hold the pole grip with the tip on the ground beside your foot, close to the body, and adjust the length until your elbow forms a right angle, with the forearm parallel to the ground. That 90 degree elbow is the position from which the arm can both push down effectively and swing freely, and it is the fit recommended almost universally by manufacturers, guides, and physical therapists. Check both arms, people are more asymmetric than they think, and set both poles identically for flat travel.

If you are buying poles or setting them for someone else without the chance to stand and measure, a reliable arithmetic shortcut exists: multiply height in centimeters by about 0.68 to get pole length in centimeters. A 175 centimeter person, about five feet nine, lands near 119 centimeters, and would set adjustable poles to 120; a 160 centimeter person lands near 110; a 190 centimeter person near 130. Fixed-length poles are typically sold in five centimeter steps, commonly from 100 to 135 centimeters, and the shortcut tells you which to pick, though anyone between sizes, or anyone who hikes varied terrain, should favor adjustables precisely because this whole guide is about changing the number. Most adjustable trekking poles offer a range around 60 to 140 centimeters, with the usable adjustment marked in printed graduations on the shafts; note your personal baseline number once and setting up at any trailhead becomes a five second job instead of a posture experiment.

A few refinements make the baseline genuinely yours. First, measure with your pack on if you hike with a heavy one, since a loaded pack compresses posture slightly. Second, decide the fit at the grip you actually hold: hands should rest on the main grip with the strap supporting the wrist, not throttling the pole with a fist clenched at the very top. Third, account for tip hardware, rubber tip protectors add a centimeter or two, snow baskets change how deep the tip sinks, so verify the elbow angle with the pole equipped as it will be used. Fourth, terrain bias is legitimate: hikers who know a route is dominated by descent sometimes set the baseline a couple of centimeters long from the start, and dedicated fast walkers on smooth ground, the Nordic walking discipline, use a slightly different fit discussed later in this guide.

Finally, understand what the baseline is for, because it is often misunderstood as a rule about correctness rather than a rule about mechanics. The right-angle elbow puts the pole's plant point beside the body, where a light plant provides balance without braking, and it gives the arm room to extend backward through the push, which is where the propulsion in pole walking actually comes from. A pole set ten centimeters too long moves the plant point forward, and every plant then brakes the stride slightly, thousands of small brakings per hour. A pole set too short never gets weight into the push at all and functions as an expensive metronome. Fit once, carefully, on flat ground, memorize the number on the shaft, and every adjustment in the rest of this guide becomes plus or minus a known quantity from a known starting point.

sections.heading: Anatomy of an Adjustable Pole: Sections, Grips, Straps, Baskets, and Tips
sections.body:
Adjusting poles intelligently is easier when you know what the pieces are and what each contributes. A typical adjustable trekking pole is built from two or three telescoping shaft sections of aluminum or carbon fiber. Aluminum, commonly a 7075-series alloy, is the workhorse: slightly heavier, but it survives abuse by bending, and a bent aluminum pole can often be straightened enough in the field to finish a trip. Carbon fiber is lighter and stiffer and damps vibration pleasantly, but it fails differently, when overloaded or crushed against rock it can crack or shatter outright, which is worth remembering when jamming poles between boulders or flying with them unprotected. Three-section poles collapse shorter for packing; two-section poles are marginally stiffer and lighter for their strength. A separate family, folding poles, uses three or four short sections joined by an internal cord, tensioned like an avalanche probe and secured with a push-button; they pack smallest of all, and most offer only a short adjustment range near the grip, typically 15 to 20 centimeters, which is still enough for every technique in this guide.

The grip and strap are the interface that determines whether pole force actually reaches the ground. Grips come in cork, which molds to the hand and manages sweat well; EVA foam, the lightest and most comfortable in heat; and rubber, which insulates in cold and suits winter use but chafes bare sweaty hands in summer. The detail that matters most for terrain technique is the grip extension: a secondary sleeve of foam below the main grip, standard on mountain-oriented poles. That lower grip exists precisely so that you can choke down, sliding the hand lower on the pole for a steep step or a sidehill without stopping to change the pole's set length; when buying poles for varied terrain, treat the extension as close to mandatory. Straps are load-bearing equipment, not tethers, and an entire later section covers using them correctly.

At the working end, the shaft carries a basket and a tip. Baskets are the small discs that stop the pole plunging past its useful depth: minimal trekking baskets of a few centimeters for three-season trail use, where their job is mainly to keep the tip from wedging deep between rocks and roots, and wide powder baskets, eight to ten centimeters or more, for snow, where they provide the flotation that makes a pole useful at all. Baskets screw or snap on and should be matched to the season; carrying snow baskets in the pack costs almost nothing on a shoulder-season trip. Tips themselves are carbide or hardened steel, and they bite rock astonishingly well, better slightly dulled than needle-sharp. Rubber tip covers exist for pavement, slickrock, and indoor transport, and etiquette-sensitive or erosion-sensitive areas sometimes request them; carry them, they weigh grams.

Understand one printed marking above all: the maximum-extension line, usually labeled STOP or MAX, near the top of each lower section. Extending a section past that line leaves too little shaft overlapping inside the joint, and the joint will flex, slip, or break exactly when weighted hard. If reaching your baseline length forces any section past its stop line, the poles are too short for you; the fix is different poles, not optimism. Within legal range, distribute length reasonably evenly between sections rather than maxing one and collapsing another, the pole is stiffer that way, and note that on three-section poles many hikers set the lower section once and make all terrain adjustments with the upper joint only, which is faster and keeps a known reference.

sections.heading: Shortening for the Climb: Uphill Adjustments and Technique
sections.body:
When the trail tilts upward, the ground rises toward your hands, and a pole set for flat ground becomes functionally too long: plants land high, elbows fold past the strong right angle, shoulders hike toward the ears, and the arms lose the leverage to push. The correction is to shorten. The working rule, echoed by essentially every manufacturer and mountain guiding organization, is to shorten poles by about 5 to 10 centimeters for a sustained climb, with the amount scaled to the slope: a gentle grade might want only 5 centimeters, a steep sustained climb 10, and a very steep direct ascent 15. The test of correctness is the same as the baseline test, applied to the slope you are on: planting the pole a comfortable half step ahead, your elbow should again sit near a right angle, forearm near level. If your elbow is sharply closed and your hand is near your shoulder, the pole is still too long; if you are reaching down at a straight arm, you have overcorrected.

Shortened correctly, poles change what climbing feels like, because the arms become working members rather than passengers. Plant the pole roughly even with the opposite foot or a little ahead, then push down and back through the grip as you step, finishing the push as the hand passes the hip. The rhythm for most walkers is the natural alternating gait, right pole with left foot, and it should feel like the poles are helping lift body weight uphill, which they genuinely are; studies of pole walking uphill show meaningful transfer of work to the upper body, at the cost of slightly higher total energy expenditure and heart rate, a trade most hikers happily accept because the legs, the limiting resource, are spared. On very steep pitches or big single steps, switch momentarily to a double plant: both poles planted together uphill, then push through both while the legs make two quick steps, a technique that also serves beautifully on staircase-style trails.

Short, steep, and broken climbs often change grade every few meters, and stopping to re-adjust at every roll would be absurd. This is where choking up on the grip does the work of a length change: for a brief steep section, simply slide the hands down onto the grip extensions, effectively shortening the poles by 10 or 15 centimeters instantly, then return to the main grips when the grade eases. Reserve actual lock adjustments for sustained changes, a climb you expect to last more than roughly ten or fifteen minutes, and let the hands handle everything shorter. One more grip note for climbing: it is fine, and often best, to come out of the straps or wear them loose uphill, since the push is downward and the strap contributes less than it does on the flat.

A few uphill errors are worth naming because they are nearly universal among new pole users. Planting too far ahead turns each plant into a brake and each push into a pull-up; keep plants beside or slightly ahead of the body. Death-gripping the pole wastes forearm strength; the push should ride through the base of the hand and the strap, fingers relaxed. Letting the poles trail and click behind you means the length or the technique has failed, and you are carrying, not using, them. And leaning heavily on poles to drag yourself up sustained grades is a posture error: the body should stay tall over the feet, hips forward, with poles assisting rhythm and adding push, because a climber folded over their poles has traded lung capacity for the illusion of support.

sections.heading: Lengthening for the Descent: Downhill Adjustments and Technique
sections.body:
Descent is where poles earn their keep, and it is also where correct length matters most. Going downhill, the ground drops away from your hands, so a pole at flat-ground length forces you to bend forward to reach the trail, and a forward-bent hiker on a descent is a hazard to themselves: weight tips onto the toes, the view of foot placements shortens, and any slip accelerates into a headlong stumble. The correction is the mirror of the climb: lengthen poles by about 5 to 10 centimeters for a sustained descent, more, up to 15, when the grade is severe. Correct length lets you stand tall, slightly back on your heels as good descent posture demands, and still plant the tips comfortably ahead and below without reaching. The elbow check works here too: planting downslope ahead of you, the arm should meet the pole with a comfortable, slightly open bend, never locked straight and never folded tight.

Downhill technique differs fundamentally from uphill: poles now absorb and steady rather than propel. Plant earlier and further ahead than on the flat, placing the tip before or as the leading foot lands so the pole is already sharing load during the knee's hardest moment, the braking phase of each downhill step. This is where the documented reduction in knee joint loading comes from, forces measured at the knee drop meaningfully when a portion of each impact routes through the arms, and over a long mountain descent that redistribution is the difference between arriving with tired shoulders or wrecked quadriceps and knees. On steep or loose descents, use the double plant liberally: both poles planted below, weight shared onto them, then one or two controlled steps down between the poles, repeat. It is slower and vastly more secure, and it is the standard technique for scree, wet rock slabs at a walkable angle, and eroded step-downs.

Big single drops, boulder steps, water bars, deserve their own habit: plant both poles below the step, lean weight into the grips, and lower yourself with the arms assisting the front leg's eccentric work. For this move many hikers momentarily palm the pole tops, resting the heel of the hand on the grip's crown for a straighter push, which is comfortable exactly when poles have been lengthened properly. Loose surfaces reward a slightly wider plant stance, tips out to the sides rather than directly in the line of travel, so a skidding tip does not cross your feet.

The cautions are as important as the techniques. Do not overload a single planted pole on steep ground; poles are balance and load-sharing devices, and a lone pole taking full body weight can skate off rock or punch through soft ground without warning. On descents among boulders, tree roots, or crevices, be deliberate about where tips go, a tip trapped in a crack while your body continues downhill is the classic mechanism for both broken poles and wrenched shoulders, and it is the main reason the strap section of this guide tells you when to take hands out entirely. Check your locks before the descent begins: a section that slips under load is merely annoying uphill and genuinely dangerous downhill, so give each joint a firm push-test at the top. And if the descent steepens into terrain where you want your hands, real scrambling, ladders, chains, do not compromise: collapse the poles, stow them on the pack, and use the rock. Recognizing the moment poles stop helping is itself a pole skill, and the descent is where that judgment is most often tested.

sections.heading: Sidehills and Traverses: Handling Ground That Tilts Across Your Path
sections.body:
A traverse, a path crossing a slope rather than running straight up or down it, presents the one situation where your two poles want to be two different lengths. The ground under your uphill hand is higher than the ground under your downhill hand, sometimes dramatically so on a steep sidehill, and poles set identically will leave the uphill arm jammed and shrugged while the downhill arm dangles and reaches. There are two solutions, and choosing between them is a matter of how long the traverse lasts. For a long, sustained traverse, an old switchbacking road cut, a slope-crossing section you can see running ahead for kilometers, actually re-set the poles asymmetrically: shorten the uphill pole roughly 5 to 10 centimeters and lengthen the downhill pole by a similar amount, scaled to the slope's tilt. Set correctly, both elbows return to their comfortable angles, the shoulders sit level, and you can stride normally with both poles genuinely working.

For everything shorter, and most traverses are shorter, do not touch the locks at all: use your grips. Choke down on the uphill pole, sliding that hand onto the grip extension or even the upper shaft, and keep the downhill hand on the main grip, palming the very top of the grip if a little extra reach helps. This instantly creates the asymmetry the ground demands and just as instantly undoes itself when the trail turns. This is the single most valuable use of grip extensions, and on switchbacking trails, where the slope changes sides at every turn, it is the only sane method, swapping the choked hand at each switchback corner as the uphill side alternates. Hands should be loose in the straps or out of them on the uphill side when choked down, since a hand below the strap's anchor point cannot use it anyway.

Technique on a traverse is about respecting where the real support is. Your uphill pole tip lands close to your feet and mostly steadies; your downhill pole is the one preventing the fall that matters, the tumble down the slope, so give the downhill plant your attention: place it firmly, slightly ahead, on ground you trust, and time your steps so that the downhill pole is planted whenever your downhill foot is loaded. On soft sidehills, mud, wet grass over hardpan, scree, the downhill tip may need a deliberate stab to seat it. Keep your body weight over your feet with edged boot placements doing the real work; leaning into the hillside feels safer but actually rolls your soles off their edges and is the classic cause of sidehill slips. The poles enable the correct, slightly counterintuitive posture, torso upright, weight on the feet, by giving your hands the confidence not to grope for the slope.

Two special cases complete the picture. Crossing a short steep gully or crossing spring snowfields on a traverse, many walkers briefly bring both hands to the downhill technique: both poles planted on the downhill side in sequence, body always between slope and poles, moving one contact at a time so that three points, two feet and a pole, or two poles and a foot, hold the ground whenever anything moves. And on a traverse with serious exposure, where a slip would not be a sit-down but a long slide, apply the recurring judgment of this guide: consider whether poles are still the right tool, because on genuinely steep hard snow that role belongs to an ice axe, and no pole length compensates for carrying the wrong equipment onto the wrong slope.

sections.heading: Flat Ground and Fast Walking: Pole Length for Distance and Nordic Technique
sections.body:
Flat and rolling ground is where most pole hours are actually spent, and the baseline right-angle fit from earlier in this guide is the correct setting for ordinary hiking there. But flat ground has its own refinement culture, imported from Nordic walking, the fitness discipline that grew out of cross-country ski training in Finland and spread across Europe in the late 1990s, and its lessons transfer directly to any hiker who wants to cover distance efficiently. The Nordic convention sizes poles at about 0.68 times height, essentially the same arithmetic as the trekking baseline, with fit fine-tuned so the elbow is at or just below ninety degrees; some faster practitioners size a touch longer, closer to 0.70 times height, because the technique emphasizes a long push-off behind the body, and a slightly longer pole extends that push. If your interest is exercise walking on tracks and smooth trails, err a centimeter or two long; if it is all-day hiking economy, stay at baseline.

What distinguishes flat-ground technique is the push phase. On the flat, the pole plants beside the body, roughly level with the heel of the opposite foot, angled backward, never vertically and never ahead, and the work is a push down and back that continues as the arm swings past the hip, with the hand opening slightly at the end of the push so the pole trails for an instant before the swing forward. All meaningful propulsion happens behind you. This is where straps become genuinely load-bearing: a correctly set strap lets the open hand keep driving through the pole at the end of the stroke, which is why dedicated Nordic walking poles have glove-like strap harnesses. The gait is the natural cross-pattern, right arm with left foot, at your ordinary arm swing rhythm; if the arms and legs fall into same-side pacing, stop, dangle the poles by their straps, walk normally until the natural swing re-establishes, and let the poles rejoin it.

The payoff on the flat is not knee protection, there is little braking load to share, but posture, rhythm, and workload distribution. Poles used actively on the flat raise heart rate and calorie expenditure noticeably compared to unpoled walking at the same speed, research on Nordic walking commonly finds increases in the range of 15 to 25 percent, while, importantly, perceived exertion rises much less, because the added work is spread across the upper body. For a loaded backpacker, active flat-ground poling also meters out a steady rhythm that eats kilometers, keeps hands elevated and moving, which reduces the finger swelling many hikers get on long days, and maintains the torso in a tall, open posture late into the day when tired walkers slump.

Flat terrain also invites the one legitimate lazy option: not using the poles. On smooth ground with a light load, carrying poles collapsed on the pack, or holding both in one hand mid-shaft like a baton, is perfectly reasonable, and cycling between active poling and carrying is a normal rhythm on mixed routes. What is worth avoiding is the third state, poles dangling from the wrists and clicking along unweighted, which combines the drag of carrying with none of the benefit and adds the small but real hazard of a loose tip finding a crack mid-stride. Decide at any given moment whether the poles are working or riding; both are fine, and the discipline of choosing keeps flat ground from turning good equipment into noise.

sections.heading: Snowshoeing and Winter Travel: Pole Length on Snow
sections.body:
Snow rewrites the pole-length rules, because the surface itself gives way. The first and non-negotiable change is hardware: swap the small trekking baskets for wide powder baskets, eight to ten centimeters across or more, before the first snowy outing of the season. Without them a pole plunges until the grip meets the snow, which is not support but comedy, and a basketless pole driven deep and then levered forward is how shafts get bent. With powder baskets fitted, the working rule for snowshoeing is to set poles a little longer than your summer baseline, commonly 5 to 10 centimeters longer, because even with baskets the tips sink into all but the firmest snow, and because snowshoes themselves add a couple of centimeters of standing height while soft snow subtracts more beneath them. The familiar elbow test remains the arbiter, applied on the snow you are actually standing on: hand on grip, tip planted and settled to its working depth, elbow near a right angle.

Snow travel also demands more re-adjustment during a single outing than any summer hiking, because the effective surface changes hour by hour: a wind-packed morning crust that barely takes a tip becomes knee-deep mush by afternoon, and a shaded north slope and a sunny south slope on the same hill are different surfaces entirely. Adjustable poles are close to mandatory in winter for this reason, and lever locks, operable with gloved hands, are strongly preferable to twist locks, which demand grip strength and bare-hand dexterity exactly when you have neither. Practice adjusting your specific poles with your winter gloves on, at home, once; it is a two-minute rehearsal that pays off on every cold summit ridge.

The terrain corrections from the summer sections apply on snow with the same logic and slightly larger numbers. Shorten for sustained climbs; on steep snowshoe ascents where you kick steps straight up the fall line, shorten aggressively or choke down hard, and drive the tips in with each step for a four-point crawl rhythm. Lengthen for descents, where poles planted below you check speed and keep the torso upright as snowshoe tails skid. On sidehill traverses, the choke-down method rules, with one winter-specific caution: on firm, steep snow, a slipped snowshoer accelerates fast, and poles will not arrest a real slide, that is what an ice axe and the knowledge to use it are for. Treat poles on steep hard snow as balance aids only, and choose routes accordingly.

Deep unbroken powder adds its own techniques. Breaking trail, lengthen the poles slightly and plant them well forward; they double as probes for buried logs, rocks, and creek voids, a genuine hazard-detection role, and a pole that suddenly finds no bottom is telling you something important about the next step. When you flounder or fall in deep snow, and everyone does, cross both poles flat on the surface and push up on the X they form, distributing your weight the way the snowshoe does; pushing on a single upright pole just drills it toward the earth's core. Two final winter habits: clear wet snow that balls onto baskets and tips with a tap of pole on pole rather than a glove, and at day's end, pull the sections apart and dry them indoors, because meltwater trapped inside a closed aluminum pole over a winter is how corrosion quietly welds the sections together. Skiers and splitboarders inherit all of the above plus their own conventions, but for the snowshoer and winter hiker, the summary is simple: bigger baskets, a bit more length, lever locks, gloves-on practice, and respect for what poles cannot do on steep hard snow.

sections.heading: Straps: How to Wear Them, How They Carry Load, and When to Take Your Hands Out
sections.body:
The wrist strap is the most misused part of the trekking pole, and using it correctly changes what the pole can do. Most people put their hand through the loop from the top and grab the grip, which produces a strap that either does nothing or garrotes the wrist. The correct method comes from ski poles: bring your hand up through the loop from below, so the strap lies across the back of the wrist and its two webbing strands pass under the palm, then take the grip so that you are holding both the grip and the strap webbing together, with the strap supported between thumb and forefinger. Adjust the strap length so that, held this way, your hand sits naturally at its normal position on the grip with the strap snug but not tight. Set up like this, the strap becomes a sling that transmits your push into the pole through the heel of the hand and wrist, which means the fingers can stay almost completely relaxed. That is the entire secret of all-day pole comfort: the hand rides, the strap works, and forearm fatigue and blisters largely disappear. It also means you can open your hand entirely at the end of a stride, or to grab a map, a camera, or a snack, without dropping the pole; it hangs from the strap, instantly recoverable.

Strap length deserves a real fitting session. Too loose, and the strap sags below the palm and transmits nothing; you will find yourself clutching the grip again within minutes. Too tight, and the strap forces the hand high on the grip, chafes, and restricts blood flow to cold fingers in winter. Fit straps wearing the gloves of the season, bare hands in summer, liner or shell gloves in winter, which usually means re-adjusting twice a year; most straps adjust by a simple pull-through buckle hidden at the grip, and better poles let you do it in seconds. If a strap edge rubs the back of your hand raw on a long day, flip the strap so its padded or seamless face lies against skin, most are directional and half the world wears them inverted.

Now the other half of strap wisdom: knowing when to get your hands out. A strapped pole is an extension of your skeleton, which is exactly what you do not want when the pole can be seized by the world while your body keeps moving. The classic situations, worth committing to memory as a checklist, are these. Stream and river crossings: a pole trapped between boulders in current, with your wrist strapped to it, can anchor you in the one place you must not stop, and a strapped pole under water is genuinely difficult to escape; cross with hands out of straps, gripping bare. Scrambling and boulder fields: a tip wedged in a crack as you move can dislocate a shoulder or slam you onto rock; hands out, or better, poles stowed. Avalanche terrain: every avalanche safety curriculum teaches skiing and snowshoeing without pole straps in hazardous terrain, because in a slide, strapped poles anchor you in the moving snow, prevent swimming motions, and drag you deeper. Dense timber and brush, where tips snag constantly, and any descent so steep that a snagged pole would pitch you forward, get the same treatment.

The habit to build is a two-second transition: thumbs flick out of the straps at the top of a crossing or scramble, back in on the far side. Hikers who have practiced the correct up-from-below strap entry can do this without looking. Straps, used this way, are not a safety compromise; they are load-bearing equipment with a clearly defined off switch, and knowing both halves, how to load them and when to shed them, is what separates practiced pole users from people the poles occasionally injure.

sections.heading: Locking Mechanisms: Lever Locks, Twist Locks, and Keeping Poles from Slipping
sections.body:
A pole that changes length under load is worse than no adjustment at all, so the locks deserve understanding and occasional maintenance. Adjustable poles use one of a few mechanisms. The most common on modern poles is the external lever lock, marketed under names like FlickLock and Speed Lock: a cam-action clamp around the joint that squeezes the outer tube onto the inner one when the lever is closed. Lever locks are visible, glove-friendly, fast, and easy to diagnose, and they hold with great force, which is why they have taken over the market. Their one maintenance need is tension: each lever has a small adjustment screw or dial, and the correct setting is the tension at which the lever snaps closed with firm thumb pressure and the joint then cannot be telescoped by a hard push. If a lever closes effortlessly, it is too loose and the pole will slip under body weight, tighten the screw a quarter turn and retest; if you cannot close it with a thumb, back the screw off slightly. Check tension at the trailhead, and expect to touch the screws a couple of times a season, since plastic parts relax and temperatures change the fit.

The older mechanism is the internal twist lock: rotating the pole sections relative to each other drives a small expander plug outward against the inside of the outer tube, jamming the joint by friction. Twist locks are sleek and have no external parts to snag, but they carry known vices. They demand grip strength, are miserable with cold or gloved hands, and they fail in characteristic ways: over-tightened until the expander seizes and the sections spin uselessly, or contaminated with water, grit, or, fatally, lubricant, after which they will not bite at all. Never oil or grease a twist-lock pole; the mechanism is friction, and lubricating it is disabling it. If a twist lock spins without engaging, pull the sections fully apart, you may need to unscrew the expander by hand a turn or two so it can re-engage, wipe both the plug and the tube interior dry and clean, then reassemble and tighten with the sections aligned. Folding poles use a third scheme, an internal tension cord with a push-button catch, plus usually one small lever-lock zone for length adjustment near the grip; their failure mode is a stretched or iced cord that leaves the joints slightly soft, and their discipline is simply to confirm the button has fully clicked home before weighting the pole.

Whatever the mechanism, adopt the load test as a ritual: after any adjustment, and always before a descent, set the pole vertical, put both hands on the grip, and give it a hard shove downward with real body weight behind it. Three seconds per pole. A joint that survives the shove will survive the trail; a joint that slips just told you at the trailhead instead of on a wet rock step. While testing, glance at the maximum-extension marks, every section must show its overlap zone respected, and check that sections are distributed sensibly rather than one joint carrying all the extension.

Locks are also where poles quietly age. Grit works into joints on dusty and muddy trails, and salt does in coastal and winter use; the cure is the maintenance routine in this guide's final section, but the symptom appears at the lock first, sections that grind as they slide, levers that need ever more tension, twist locks that catch inconsistently. Treat any new slipping behavior as a maintenance flag rather than something to compensate for with brute tightening, because the escalation path, cranking a lever screw to its limit, over-torquing a twist expander, ends in cracked clamps and seized poles, both of which are field-trip-ending failures that ten minutes of cleaning would have prevented.

sections.heading: Stream Crossings, Scrambles, and Stowing: When to Re-Rig and When to Put Poles Away
sections.body:
Certain terrain features demand a deliberate change of rig rather than a length tweak, and stream crossings head the list. For any crossing beyond a rock-hop, stop and reconfigure. Lengthen both poles somewhat if the water is more than shin deep, you will be reaching down past your feet to the streambed, take both hands fully out of the straps for the reasons the strap section details, and if you are carrying a pack with a hip belt, unbuckle it so the pack can be shed instantly in a fall. Face slightly upstream and move with two points always planted: plant both poles upstream, sidestep, re-plant. The poles probe depth, read the invisible bottom, and brace against the current's push, and a third point of contact in moving water is worth more than it is anywhere else in hiking. Respect the hard limits: fast water above the knees is dangerous for most people regardless of poles, and no pole technique makes an unwise crossing wise; the strongest crossing decision is often to walk upstream for a better ford or turn around.

Scrambling, terrain steep enough to want hands on rock, poses the opposite problem: the poles themselves become the hazard. A pole in the hand on real scrambling terrain occupies the exact resource the terrain demands, and a strapped pole snagging in a crack while you are committed to a move is a recognized cause of shoulder injuries and falls. The rule is simple: when you want your hands, stow the poles, and do it before the difficulty starts, at the base of the rock band rather than halfway up it. Collapse them to minimum length or fold them, and fix them to the pack, under compression straps diagonally across the back panel, or in the dedicated pole carriers many packs provide. Stow tips down or padded; a tip standing above your shoulder can catch overhead rock and, on a fall, becomes a spear beside your head. For terrain that alternates quickly, walking with short scrambly steps every few minutes, an intermediate rig works: collapse both poles, hold the pair in one hand at mid-shaft like a baton, and keep the other hand free; it is remarkable how much easy scrambling can be done carrying poles this way without a full stow.

A few other re-rigging moments recur on real routes. Ladders, chains, and via-ferrata-style fixtures: full stow, always, both hands on the hardware. Extended talus and boulder-hopping: many experienced hikers stow or baton the poles here even though slopes are moderate, because tip-trap terrain is exactly where poles snag, and rhythm hopping between blocks is a hands-and-eyes activity. Very narrow ledge trails with a rock wall on one side: consider carrying both poles in the outside hand, keeping the wall-side hand free to trail the rock. Bushwhacking through dense brush: baton or stow, since extended poles in undergrowth are anchors. In all cases the underlying skill is the same, noticing the transition. Terrain changes announce themselves a few steps ahead, and the practiced pole user makes the rig change at the announcement, standing somewhere comfortable, rather than negotiating a strap-tangle mid-crux.

Finally, make stowing itself a practiced operation. At home, time how long it takes to go from poles-in-hand to poles-secured-on-pack and back; if either direction takes more than a minute or requires taking the pack off, rig a better attachment now, because a stow that is annoying will be skipped in the field, and skipped stows are how poles end up in hands on terrain where they do not belong. The goal state is casual competence: length changes in seconds, strap exits by reflex, and a stow so easy that the decision to make it is never resisted.

sections.heading: Technique on the Move: Planting, Rhythm, and Making Adjustments Without Stopping
sections.body:
Length settings create the possibility of good technique; rhythm realizes it. The foundational gait with poles is the alternating pattern the body already owns: the right arm swings with the left leg, so the right pole plants as the left foot lands, and vice versa. Do not construct this consciously, walk naturally and let the poles join the arm swing that is already there, planting each pole roughly beside the opposite foot, angled slightly back, and pushing through as the body passes over. New users who find themselves in same-side lockstep, right pole with right foot, a surprisingly stable but inefficient pattern, should not fight it mid-stride; dangle both poles by their straps, walk twenty natural steps, and re-engage. The alternating pattern gives two ground contacts through almost every phase of gait and distributes pole work evenly, and once grooved it costs no attention at all, which is the point: pole technique that requires thinking about steals attention from foot placement, where attention belongs.

Above the base rhythm sit the deliberate patterns, chosen for the moment. The double plant, both poles together, is for big steps up or down, brief steep pitches, and moments of doubt, a puddle-margin, a wobbly rock, an icy patch, where planting both tips and keeping them loaded while the feet solve the problem converts a two-point creature into a braced tripod. Parallel poling, planting both poles every second stride like a cross-country skier, suits fast flat travel and gentle downhill cruising on smooth trails. And single-pole moments are legitimate: on a narrow trail with brush against one shoulder, or contouring with one hand occupied, shift both poles to one hand or work one pole in the double role, planting it center-line with each stride. None of these are formal exercises; they are options that become reflexes with a few outings.

The skill that ties this guide together is adjusting without breaking stride, because terrain rarely waits for a maintenance stop. The hierarchy runs from instant to deliberate. Instant: choking up or down on the grip and its extension, the always-available five-to-fifteen-centimeter correction, and palming the grip top for a single tall step down. Seconds: strap exits and entries, practiced until they happen with a flick while walking. Half a minute, stationary: actual lock adjustments, done at the natural pause points a route offers, the top of the descent, the bottom of the climb, the bank of the stream, the edge of the snowfield. Read the route ahead and batch your changes at those seams; a party that adjusts at the seams never stops for poles anywhere else. When you do stop to adjust, use the printed scale, your baseline number plus or minus the standard corrections, rather than re-deriving the elbow angle from scratch each time, and set both poles before moving, since one long and one short pole on straight terrain quietly torques the shoulders for kilometers.

Last, calibrate how much force poles are meant to carry, because both extremes are common errors. Poles are not crutches on ordinary ground: on good trail the plant is light, a rhythm touch and a modest push, and the legs remain the engine. Nor are they ornaments on hard ground: on the steep descent or the loaded stream crossing they should be carrying genuine weight, arms working, and a user who has never felt their triceps after a big descent has been under-using the equipment. The right mental model is a continuously variable four-wheel drive, torque flowing to the arms exactly in proportion to what the terrain asks, and length, rhythm, and grip position are the three levers that make the flow smooth.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Quick Field Fixes
sections.body:
Most pole problems in the field trace to a short list of causes, and diagnosing by symptom is quick once the list is known. Aching shoulders or neck by mid-morning almost always means poles set too long or gripped too high: the shoulders are riding shrugged, thousands of plants have each lifted the shoulder girdle a centimeter. Fix by dropping length two to five centimeters below whatever felt right in the shop, relaxing the hands into properly fitted straps, and consciously letting the shoulder blades settle once per water break until the posture holds itself. Sore forearms and hot spots on the palms mean the straps are not carrying load, the fingers have been clenching all day; re-rig the straps hand-up-from-below, snug them so the push rides the wrist, and let the fingers go soft. A pole that gradually creeps shorter over an hour is a lock problem: a lever needing a quarter turn of tension, or a twist lock that was spun tight in haste without seating; fix at the next pause and load-test properly. A tip that skates on rock instead of biting is either a worn-smooth carbide tip, replaceable, most brands sell tip kits that press or screw on, or a rubber tip protector left on from the parking lot, which on wet rock is a genuine slip hazard and should come off at the trailhead.

Technique errors have their own signatures. Tips clicking along behind you, never weighted, means the poles have become jewelry, usually because the terrain is easy; either engage them with the flat-ground push technique or stow them honestly. Plants landing far ahead of the body and jolting the elbow mean over-reaching, often from poles set too long; the plant belongs beside the opposite foot on the flat, ahead only on descents. Tripping on your own poles in rocky ground means the tips are wandering across your line of travel, keep plants outside the rails of an imaginary track the width of your hips. Poles crossing behind you on switchback turns, a classic tangle, is cured by the corner habit: as you enter a switchback, plant the inside pole once at the apex and pivot around it. And a party member white-knuckling both poles downhill, arms rigid, torso pitched back, is a length problem wearing a fear costume: lengthen their poles properly, and the posture usually fixes itself because reaching the ground no longer requires leaning.

Equipment failures in the field have field-grade answers. A bent aluminum section can usually be coaxed straight enough to telescope by bracing it across the knee or between two rocks and bending gently in stages, expect a scar and plan on replacement, but the trip continues. A cracked carbon section cannot be trusted with load again; splint it if it must carry any weight, hose clamps or tent-pole sleeve and tape, or retire that pole to pack duty and finish the day with one. A seized twist lock, sections spinning freely, is fixed by separating the sections completely, drying and de-gritting the expander plug, backing it off a turn, and reassembling. Lost baskets on snow can be improvised with a disc of closed-cell foam pad or a stout stick lashed as a crossbar above the tip. A torn strap becomes a loop of cord for the day. Almost nothing about a trekking pole is fatal to a trip if the user is calm and has tape, cord, and the willingness to walk out with asymmetric equipment.

The overarching fix, though, is preventive: the thirty-second trailhead ritual. Set both poles to your known baseline number, snap and load-test every lock, confirm straps are entered correctly and sized to today's gloves, check that tips are bare or covered as today's surface demands, and glance at baskets against today's season. Hikers with the ritual almost never experience the mid-descent slip, the mile of shoulder shrug, or the strap-tangled scramble, and the ritual costs less time than reading this paragraph did.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance: Keeping Adjustable Poles Adjustable
sections.body:
Adjustability is a mechanical property, and it survives exactly as long as the joints are clean, dry, and within their design tension. The single most important habit costs one minute: after any wet, muddy, snowy, or coastal outing, separate the pole sections fully, wipe them, and let them dry apart, overnight indoors is ideal, before reassembling. Water trapped inside a closed pole is the primary killer of adjustable poles: in aluminum it feeds corrosion that swells and pits the tube walls until sections grind and finally seize; in poles left wet through a freezing night it becomes ice that locks the joints outright; and in twist-lock poles it lubricates the expander into uselessness at the worst moment. Sand and grit are the second enemy, working into joints on dusty trails and grinding the tubes as they telescope; the cure is the same disassembly plus a wipe of both the inner tube surfaces and, on twist locks, the expander plug, using a dry or barely damp cloth. Never lubricate the adjustment mechanisms of any pole, no oil, no silicone spray, no wax on the gripping zones; every locking system relies on friction, and lubricant converts a locking pole into a collapsing one. If sections slide roughly after cleaning, very fine steel wool or an abrasive pad on visible corrosion spots, followed by a thorough wipe, restores smoothness.

Inspect on a schedule tied to use, monthly in a heavy season is plenty. Run each section through your hands feeling for dents, cracks, and raised corrosion; sight down each section like an arrow shaft for straightness. Check carbide tips for wear, a healthy tip is a hollow crown or a blunt point that still bites rock, and replace tips worn to a polished dome, since replacement tip kits are cheap and a skating tip is a fall generator. Check baskets for cracks at the mounting collar. Work every lever lock and confirm its closing tension, adjusting the screw as the tension section of this guide describes, and examine plastic clamp bodies for the white stress lines that precede cracking; most manufacturers sell replacement lever assemblies, expanders, straps, and tips, and better poles are designed to be rebuilt part by part, which is worth remembering before retiring a pole over a two-dollar component. Straps deserve a glance at their stitching and their buckle teeth, and folding poles need their tension cords checked for fray where the cord enters each joint.

Storage and transport have their own small rules. Store poles fully dry, with lever locks closed loosely or twist locks left just barely snug, in a dry indoor space; a garage that freezes and sweats through the seasons ages poles fast, and long-term storage compressed with locks cranked tight fatigues the mechanisms. For air travel, poles must go in checked luggage, security regulations treat them as prohibited in cabins, and carbon poles in particular should travel padded inside a duffel or hard case, since crushing in baggage handling is the classic origin of the hairline crack that fails a month later on a descent. In a vehicle, keep poles out of the rear-window sun shelf; summer dashboard temperatures soften grip adhesives and warp plastic clamp parts.

A note on lifespan and judgment closes the subject. Aluminum poles with maintained locks routinely serve for a decade or more, accumulating honest scars; carbon poles serve as long if never crushed or deeply gouged, but any carbon section that has taken a hard point impact, a rockfall strike, a car door, a baggage crush, should be flexed and inspected with suspicion and retired on reasonable doubt, because carbon conceals its damage and announces it by snapping under load. Retire any section that no longer holds under the trailhead load test after cleaning and tension adjustment, whatever its age. The economics favor care overwhelmingly: a few minutes of drying and a seasonal half hour of inspection preserve equipment whose entire value, as this guide has argued from the first section, is that its length can be trusted, changed, and trusted again, on every slope of every outing.

guides.title: Using Trekking Poles Effectively
guides.summary: How to choose, size and adjust trekking poles, use the straps correctly, and pole efficiently on flat ground, uphill, downhill, sidehills, stream crossings, snow and scree, plus maintenance, repairs and common mistakes.

sections.heading: Why Use Trekking Poles: What They Actually Do for Your Body
sections.body:
Trekking poles turn a hiker from a two-legged walker into a four-limbed one, and the benefits follow directly from that extra contact with the ground. The first and best-documented benefit is load sharing on descents. Walking downhill forces your knees and quadriceps to absorb your body weight, plus your pack, arriving with extra momentum on every single step; researchers who have instrumented hikers report that planting poles reduces the compressive and shear forces on the knee joint during steep downhill walking measurably, with one frequently cited biomechanics study from 1999 by Hermann Schwameder and colleagues finding reductions in external knee joint forces on the order of twelve to twenty-five percent on a steep grade. Over a single step that is trivial; over a ten-mile day with five thousand feet of descent, it is tens of thousands of steps, and the cumulative sparing is why long-distance hikers with decades on their knees are so often evangelists for poles.

The second benefit is stability. Two extra contact points widen your base of support dramatically, which matters most exactly when footing is worst: wet roots, greasy rock, loose gravel, mud, snow patches, stream cobbles, and the wobbly late-afternoon miles when your stabilizing muscles are tired. Falls are the leading cause of serious hiking injuries, and most falls begin as small slips that a well-planted pole converts into a stumble instead of an impact. Poles also probe: they tell you whether the bog is ankle-deep or knee-deep, whether that rock rocks, and where the bottom of a murky stream actually is, all before you commit your weight.

The third benefit is workload distribution. Poling recruits your arms, shoulders, chest and back into propulsion, which does not make walking free, in fact studies of energy expenditure generally show poles hold heart rate roughly level or raise total calorie burn slightly because more muscle is working, but it spreads fatigue across more of your body. Your legs arrive at mile twelve fresher because your arms paid part of the bill. A well-known field study by Glyn Howatson and colleagues, published in 2010, had experienced hikers ascend and descend Mount Snowdon in Wales with and without poles; the pole group reported significantly less muscle soreness and showed lower blood markers of muscle damage in the days afterward, with self-rated exertion during the hike also reduced. Reduced damage today is faster recovery tomorrow, which is the currency of multi-day trips.

There are honest costs. Poles occupy your hands, add a few hundred grams of swinging weight, require technique before they feel natural, are awkward on scrambles where you need your hands, and can be a hazard misused. Some hikers genuinely do better without them, and nobody should feel obliged. But for descents with a loaded pack, for anyone with cranky knees, hips or ankles, for balance-challenging terrain, and for the simple rhythm they lend to long flat miles, poles are among the highest-value pieces of gear in the pack, and the rest of this guide is about extracting that value with technique rather than merely carrying two sticks.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Trekking Pole: Shafts, Grips, Locks, Tips and Baskets
sections.body:
Knowing the parts of a pole makes every later decision, buying, adjusting, repairing, easier to reason about. Start at the top. The grip is where design differences matter most day to day. Cork grips mold slowly to your hand, stay comfortable in heat, and damp vibration well; genuine cork is the choice of most long-distance hikers. EVA foam is lighter, absorbs sweat, and stays comfortable when soaked, though it wears faster. Rubber grips insulate in cold and suit winter use, but they get slippery and blister-raising on hot, sweaty hands. Most grips have a slight forward cant of around fifteen degrees so your wrist stays neutral, and many poles add a short secondary grip of foam below the main one, called a choke-up grip or extension, which lets you grab the pole lower on short uphill sections or sidehills without stopping to change the length. Atop the grip sits the strap, an adjustable webbing loop whose correct use is so important, and so widely botched, that it gets its own section.

The shaft is the pole's body, made of aluminum or carbon fiber. Aluminum, typically a 7000-series alloy, is the durable workhorse: when overloaded it bends, and a bent pole can often be coaxed straight enough to finish a trip. Carbon fiber is stiffer and lighter, often saving fifty to a hundred grams per pole, and damps vibration nicely, but its failure mode is fracture: when it goes, it goes completely, sometimes leaving sharp shards, and a pole trapped between rocks and levered sideways is exactly the load it hates. Choose aluminum for hard use, rocky terrain and travel abuse; choose carbon when weight matters most and you treat gear kindly.

Adjustable poles telescope in two or three sections, held by locks. External lever locks, often called flick locks, clamp the sections with a cam you can operate with gloves on and tension with a small screw or dial; they have largely won the market because they are visible, serviceable and reliable. Internal twist locks use an expanding plug inside the shaft; they are sleeker but notorious for slipping when worn or overtightened and for seizing when gritty. Folding poles, built like tent poles from three short sections on an internal cord with a push-button lock, pack down to around thirty-five to forty-five centimeters, ideal for stowing on a pack or in luggage, at some cost in adjustability and rigidity.

At the bottom, the business end. The tip that touches rock is a small stud of tungsten carbide, hard enough to bite granite for years; it sits in a replaceable plastic tip housing that is designed to wear and, on good poles, to be pulled or heated off and renewed. Above the tip, a threaded collar accepts baskets: small trekking baskets, a few centimeters across, that stop the pole diving into mud and gaps between rocks, and wide snow baskets for winter that keep the pole from plunging through soft snow. Push-on rubber tip protectors quiet the carbide on pavement and protect rock in heavily traveled areas, and rubber walking feet, angled like tiny boot heels, suit urban fitness walking. Every one of these parts, grip, strap, sections, locks, tip housing, basket, is a consumable or a serviceable component, which is a large part of why a decent pair of poles can last decades.

sections.heading: Choosing Poles: Telescoping, Folding, Fixed Length and What to Prioritize
sections.body:
The pole market sorts into four broad families, and matching the family to your hiking is most of the buying decision. Telescoping poles, two or, more commonly, three nesting sections with lever locks, are the default choice: they adjust across a wide range, roughly sixty to one hundred forty centimeters, which supports proper uphill and downhill length changes, they accept snow baskets for winter, and their locks are field-serviceable. Their packed length, around sixty to seventy centimeters, straps to a pack fine but is awkward inside small luggage. Folding, or Z-style, poles collapse to around thirty-five to forty-five centimeters, deploy in seconds, and are the lightest full-strength option, which endears them to trail runners, travelers and anyone who stows poles often; the trade-offs are a narrower or absent adjustment range, somewhat more flex at the joints, and repairs that are less improvisable in the field. Fixed-length poles, one rigid shaft with no locks, are the lightest and stiffest of all and beloved of ultralight hikers who also use them to pitch trekking-pole tents, but you must know your length, and you give up the ability to lengthen for descents or shorten for climbs. Finally, there are ultralight compromise designs that mix carbon shafts with minimal locks; treat their weight claims kindly and their durability claims skeptically.

Beyond family, prioritize in this order. First, the lock: lever locks over twist locks, almost without exception; test that the levers snap closed with firm resistance and that a tension screw is accessible. Second, the grip and strap: hold the pole in a shop if you can, since a grip that fits your hand and a strap that adjusts smoothly matter more over a thousand miles than fifty grams of weight. Cork or foam for three-season use, rubber for winter, and check for a comfortable choke-up extension below the grip. Third, weight, which you feel in your arms on every swing: a typical aluminum telescoping pair runs around 450 to 600 grams, carbon pairs around 300 to 450, and racing designs less; swinging weight matters more than static weight, so a light lower section is worth more than a light grip. Fourth, packed length if you fly or scramble often. Fifth, price: solid aluminum pairs commonly cost a third of flagship carbon pairs and survive worse abuse.

A few specific matchings. Heavier hikers and those with big packs should favor aluminum three-section poles with robust locks. Winter users need poles that accept snow baskets and have long adjustment ranges for sidehilling. Users of trekking-pole shelters must check the shelter's required pole height, typically around 114 to 125 centimeters for many designs, and ensure their poles reach it. Travelers should note that aviation security in most countries does not allow trekking poles in carry-on baggage, so they must go in checked luggage or be bought at the destination; folding poles fit duffels best. People buying poles primarily for balance or rehabilitation may be better served by a clinician-fitted walking staff or Nordic walking poles, which have different strap systems designed for a push-and-release gait. And a single pole, or a wooden staff, remains a legitimate choice: half the benefit for half the fuss, favored by hikers who want one hand free at all times.

sections.heading: Setting the Right Length: The 90-Degree Rule and When to Break It
sections.body:
The baseline fit rule is simple: standing on flat ground in your hiking shoes, holding the grip with the tip planted beside your foot, your elbow should make a right angle, with your forearm level. That ninety-degree elbow puts the pole in the strongest, most neutral position for your wrist and shoulder and is the setting you will use for the majority of rolling trail. As a starting approximation before you fine-tune, multiplying your height in centimeters by about 0.68 lands close for most bodies: a 175-centimeter hiker usually settles near 115 to 120 centimeters of pole. Manufacturers print similar charts, roughly 100 centimeters of pole for hikers around 155 centimeters tall, 110 for 165, 120 for 178, 130 for 190, but bodies vary in torso and arm proportion, so treat charts as first guesses and the elbow as the judge. Set the length, walk fifty meters, and adjust in small increments until the pole swings naturally to a plant slightly ahead of your foot without your shoulder hiking up or your elbow opening far past ninety degrees.

On three-section poles, distribute the extension rather than maxing one section: many hikers set the lower section to a marked round number and leave it, then make all daily adjustments with the upper lock, which gives one-lever length changes on the move. Keep the printed scale visible and remember your numbers, flat, up and down, so adjustment becomes a ten-second habit instead of a fiddle. Never extend any section past its stop line, usually marked STOP or MAX; beyond it the overlap inside the shaft is too short and the pole can bend or pull apart under load.

Now the productive rule-breaking. For sustained climbing, shorten the poles five to ten centimeters from your flat setting. A shorter pole meets the rising ground at the same comfortable elbow angle and lets you press down and slightly back, adding propulsion; a pole left at flat length forces you to reach up the hill, lifting your shoulders and wasting the push. For sustained descent, lengthen five to ten centimeters, so the tips reach the lower ground ahead of you while you stay upright; on a long steep downgrade some hikers go fifteen centimeters over their flat length. For rolling terrain where stopping to adjust would be constant, split the difference or, better, use hand position: choke down onto the lower grip extension for short climbs, and press your palm on top of the grip, cupping the pommel, for short descents. Sidehill traverses call for asymmetric settings, shorter uphill hand, longer downhill hand, or simply choking up on the uphill pole.

Two checks tell you the length is wrong. If your shoulders ache or ride up near your ears, the poles are too long; if you find yourself stooping or your pole plants land behind your feet with a tapping, decorative quality, they are too short. Wrist pain often traces to length too, since a wrong length forces the wrist out of neutral on every plant. Recheck length when you change footwear, since a chunky boot versus a low trail shoe moves you a centimeter or two, and when carrying a heavy pack, which compresses posture slightly; many hikers run a centimeter or two shorter under big loads.
steps: Put on your hiking footwear, stand tall on flat ground, and hold the pole with the tip beside your foot.
Adjust length until your elbow sits at a right angle with your forearm level.
On three-section poles, set the lower section to a round marked number, then fine-tune with the upper section only.
Walk a short distance and adjust in one- or two-centimeter steps until the plant lands slightly ahead of your foot without your shoulders lifting.
Note your flat-ground number, then record two more settings: five to ten centimeters shorter for climbs and five to ten centimeters longer for descents.
Confirm no section is extended past its STOP line, and snug the lever locks so they close firmly with a definite snap.

sections.heading: Wrist Straps: The Most Misused Part of the Pole
sections.body:
Watch a random sample of hikers and most are using their straps wrongly or not at all, which throws away a large share of what poles offer. The strap is not a leash to stop a dropped pole; it is a load-bearing sling that transfers your weight from your skeleton to the pole without any grip strength at all. Used correctly, the strap carries the push and the fingers merely steer, which is the difference between arriving with relaxed hands and arriving with claw-cramped forearms and blistered palms.

The correct entry is the part everyone gets backward: bring your hand up through the loop from below, so the strap lies across the back of your wrist and its two ends pass forward under your palm, then close your hand lightly around both the grip and the webbing where it enters the grip. Now, when you press down, the heel of your hand loads the strap, and the strap hangs your weight on the pole; you can open all five fingers mid-stride and the pole stays perfectly controlled, swinging with your arm. If instead you enter from above, the strap crosses your palm, does nothing when you press down, and functions only as that leash. A correctly worn strap also self-returns the pole to your hand after each plant, which is what makes the relaxed, fingers-loose swing possible for hours.

Adjust the length so that with your hand through the loop and gripping normally, the webbing is snug enough to take load with the heel of your hand but loose enough to slip in and out without re-buckling. Most straps adjust by pulling a hidden cam or lifting a cover on top of the grip; set it once for bare hands and remember you will need to let it out for gloves in winter. Left and right straps are often shaped differently, marked L and R, with the padded face angled to lie flat against the wrist; swapped poles feel subtly wrong all day.

Now the crucial exceptions, because the same firm coupling that transfers load also transfers accidents. Take your hands completely out of the straps whenever a snagged or trapped pole could hurt you: crossing streams, where a pole wedged between rocks in current can hold your arm down or pull you off balance in exactly the place you cannot afford it; on talus, boulder fields and scrambles, where a pole jammed in a crack while you fall becomes a lever against your wrist and shoulder; in thick brush; and any time you are moving fast downhill where a sudden snag would whip you around. Skiers learn the same rule for tree runs and avalanche terrain, and it transfers directly. There is also a documented pattern of wrist and shoulder injuries, and dislocated thumbs, from falling with hands trapped in straps, since the strap prevents you from casting the pole aside to catch yourself. The habit to build is a two-position system: straps on for cruising, straps off, poles held loosely mid-shaft or in one hand, the moment terrain turns technical. Sliding in and out should be one practiced motion, and if your straps are adjusted correctly, it is.

sections.heading: Basic Technique on Flat Ground: Rhythm and the Alternating Swing
sections.body:
Good flat-ground poling is mostly rhythm, and the rhythm is one you already own: the natural arm swing of walking. Humans swing the arm opposite the striding leg, and poling simply extends that swing into the ground. As your left foot steps forward, your right arm swings forward and plants its pole; as your right foot steps, the left pole plants. This alternating pattern, identical to the diagonal stride of cross-country skiing, should feel like walking with slightly emphatic arms, not like a new skill. The most common beginner fault is overthinking it into same-side poling, right pole with right foot, which twists the torso and feels robotic; the cure is to stop thinking, drag the tips lightly for twenty meters while walking normally, let your arms fall into their native opposite-side swing, and then start planting.

The plant itself should land beside or slightly ahead of the opposite foot, tip angled slightly backward, never far out in front with the tip angled forward. A backward-angled tip lets you press down and back through the strap, and every plant then adds a small push to your stride; a forward-angled plant ahead of your body is a brake, useful on descents but pure drag on the flat. Push through the strap with the heel of the hand, fingers relaxed, and let the arm swing low and loose from the shoulder, elbow near your side, like a relaxed handshake reaching past your hip. There is no need to lift the pole high; an efficient recovery skims the tip forward a few centimeters off the ground. Your hands should stay soft enough that you could wiggle your fingers at any moment, and periodically doing exactly that is a good tension check.

On smooth, fast trail, many hikers shift to double poling for stretches: plant both poles together every second or third stride and push through them while taking two or three steps, exactly like a skier's double-pole, which recruits the whole upper body and gives the legs micro-rests. It shines on gentle downgrades and firm surfaces, and alternating between diagonal stride and occasional double poling breaks up the repetition over a long day. Another useful flat-ground variation is simply carrying the poles balanced mid-shaft in one hand during easy walking, keeping the hands free and the arms rested; poles do not have to touch the ground every step of a hike to earn their place.

Rhythm is also pace discipline. A steady pole cadence acts like a metronome, smoothing the stop-start pattern that tires hikers, and on long flats many people find their sustainable speed rises simply because the beat keeps them from dawdling and from surging. Aim for quiet: a well-planted carbide tip clicks once; a dragged or slammed pole clatters, wastes energy, and announces poor technique. Practice on an easy walk of a kilometer or two before trusting your technique on a mountain day: get the strap entry right, find the opposite-arm rhythm, tune the length, and groove the backward-angled plant. Once the pattern is automatic, your attention returns to the trail, which is where it belongs, and the poles become what they should be, background machinery that quietly saves your legs.

sections.heading: Going Uphill: Shorten, Plant and Push
sections.body:
Climbing is where poles convert your upper body into a second engine. Start with the mechanical adjustment: shorten the poles five to ten centimeters from your flat setting, more on very steep grades, or choke down onto the grip extensions. The goal is to preserve that roughly right-angled elbow when the ground in front of you is higher than the ground you stand on; poles left long force you to reach uphill, which lifts the shoulders, tips you backward and converts your push into an awkward press-up. With the length right, your hands meet the slope naturally and your posture stays tall and slightly forward, hips over feet, exactly the climbing posture you want anyway.

The stroke on a climb is a press down and back, timed with the opposite leg exactly as on the flat. Plant the tip level with or slightly behind the opposite foot, load the strap with the heel of your hand, and push as the leg drives, finishing the push past your hip. Think of pressing the mountain down and behind you. On moderate grades, the alternating rhythm carries you; on steep sustained grades many hikers shift to the double-plant technique, both poles planted together ahead, then two or three steps taken while pressing continuously through both straps, then re-plant, which pairs beautifully with the rest step, the mountaineer's habit of momentarily locking the downhill leg straight between steps to give the muscles micro-rests. Poles plus rest step is the classic sustainable formula for big climbs at altitude.

Uphill poling has real measurable value beyond propulsion. It keeps your chest more open than hunched pole-less climbing, which helps breathing; it steadies you when a step crumbles, common on eroded switchback edges; and on steps so tall they are effectively stairs, planting both poles on the step above and pressing through them takes a meaningful share of the hoist off the working quadriceps and glutes. On staircase-like terrain, shorten further or grip the poles below the heads; some hikers palm the very top of the grips on tall steps, converting the poles into a pair of low handrails.

Avoid the three classic uphill faults. First, planting too far ahead: a tip planted uphill of your hands with the shaft leaning back toward you cannot be pushed, only pulled, and pulling on a pole plant is weak and unstable; keep plants close and press down. Second, the death grip: climbing effort tempts hikers to strangle the grips, but the strap should still be doing the carrying, and clenched hands on a climb mean the strap is misadjusted or unused. Third, letting the poles shorten your stride into a shuffle by planting every single step on gentle grades; on easy climbing, planting every second stride, or double poling occasionally, keeps the stride natural and the rhythm loose.

Finally, use climbs to manage the rest of your system. Poles let you lean forward and rest your torso weight through straight arms during standing breathers, the so-called pole lean, which unloads the legs briefly without sitting down. And when a climb becomes a genuine scramble requiring hands on rock, stop and stow the poles on your pack or collapse them and carry both in one hand; a pole dangling from a strap while you grope for a hold is exactly the snag hazard the strap section warned about.

sections.heading: Going Downhill: Lengthen, Brace and Save Your Knees
sections.body:
Descents are where poles pay their fare, and technique changes more here than anywhere else. Lengthen the poles five to fifteen centimeters beyond your flat setting so the tips reach the lower ground ahead while your body stays upright; without the extra length you must stoop toward the slope, which shifts weight onto your toes and primes a header. Many hikers also shift their hands, palming the top of the grip with the pommel cupped in the palm, which lets you press straight down a long lever without bending your wrist backward. Straps can stay on for ordinary trail descents, but come out of them for steep, technical, or high-consequence downhills where a snag would be serious.

The core pattern is plant before step: the pole tips go down ahead of you, one or both, and take load as your foot descends, so each step down is a supported lowering rather than a free fall onto a bent knee. On moderate grades, keep the alternating rhythm with plants slightly ahead of each opposite foot; on steeper grades, use a double plant, both tips placed a stride ahead, then step down once or twice inside the frame the poles make, then re-plant. The poles function as movable handrails, and your triceps and lats absorb a share of every impact that would otherwise arrive at your knees and quads; this is exactly the loading the biomechanics studies measured, and over a long descent it is the difference between trembling legs and merely tired ones. Keep your knees soft and slightly bent, your steps short, and your weight centered or a touch back, and resist the descending hiker's classic error of leaning far back and skidding on heels, which poles make unnecessary.

Placement judgment matters more downhill than anywhere. Plant on surfaces that will hold: soil, gravel, the uphill side of embedded rocks. Avoid planting on wet roots, moss-slicked rock, and smooth slabs, where a carbide tip can skate exactly when you are trusting it; on such surfaces, plant in the gaps between obstacles or slow down and shorten your steps instead of trusting a dubious plant. Beware the gap trap: tips dropped between boulders or into cracks on stone staircases can wedge, and a wedged pole under load either snaps or levers your wrist, another reason straps come off on rough downhills. On steps too tall to walk, place both poles on the lower level, load them, and lower yourself with arm support, exactly the reverse of the uphill stair technique.

Two more downhill dividends deserve mention. Braking on traverses of steep grades, dragging the uphill pole tip lightly behind you like a rudder adds continuous gentle friction and confidence. And late-day protection: most downhill falls happen in the final tired hour, when proprioception fades and small stumbles stop getting caught; poles patrol exactly that failure mode, converting toe-catches and heel-skids into recovered stumbles. If your knees are the reason you bought poles, descents are where you must actually use the technique: lengthen the poles, plant before you step, and let your arms pay. Simply carrying poles downhill while stepping unsupported, a remarkably common sight, delivers almost none of the protection you paid for.
