sections.heading: Sidehills, Switchbacks and Uneven Ground
sections.body:
Real trails are rarely pure up or pure down; they traverse, contour, and switchback across slopes, and the ground under each foot is seldom the same height twice. This is where adjustable technique, more than adjustable hardware, earns its keep. On a sustained sidehill traverse, the slope rises on one side and falls on the other, so your uphill hand needs a shorter pole and your downhill hand a longer one. You can literally set different lengths, and on a long contouring section it is worth thirty seconds to do so, but the faster tool is hand position: choke down on the uphill pole, gripping the extension below the main grip or even the bare shaft, and palm the top of the downhill grip for extra reach. Keep the downhill pole planted slightly ahead as a guard rail; the consequential slip on a sidehill is always downhill, and a pre-placed downhill pole converts that slip into a lean. Swap everything at each switchback turn, which becomes automatic within an hour.

Switchback corners themselves reward a small ritual: as you enter the turn, plant the outside pole firmly at the apex and pivot your body around it, letting the pole carry you through the direction change, then re-establish the alternating rhythm on the new leg. On steep, eroded switchbacks, the corner is often the loosest ground on the trail, undercut and marbled with gravel, so slow slightly, shorten your steps, and keep one pole loaded through the whole turn.

Uneven ground, the ordinary chaos of rocks, roots, ruts and holes, calls for a looser, more improvisational style. Abandon the strict opposite-arm metronome when the terrain demands and plant wherever balance needs support: two quick plants on the same side, a wide plant to bridge a rut, a stab behind you to check a backward wobble. Keep the tips low and ready rather than swinging high. Use the poles as probes on ambiguous footing: test the rocking rock before trusting it, sound the puddle for depth, and press suspected soft ground before committing. In tall grass or leaf-drifted trail where you cannot see your feet, let the poles sweep and feel a half-step ahead of you; they will find the hidden root or the edge of the hole first, which is precisely the information your ankles want.

Boggy and muddy ground brings a specific hardware note: fit the small trekking baskets if you removed them, because a basketless tip spears half a meter into soft peat and stops you mid-stride, sometimes yanking the strap hard enough to hurt. Plant mud crossings on tussocks, stones and root masses, and keep your weight moving; standing still on soft ground is how boots get swallowed. On stepping-stone sequences, plant both poles wide for a stable A-frame and move your feet inside it, re-walking the frame forward every couple of stones.

Finally, know when the ground has beaten the tools. Boulder fields and talus, where every step is a hand-height rock and gaps wait to wedge a tip, are often faster and safer with poles collapsed and stowed, hands free for balance and the occasional touch of rock. The skill of putting poles away, quickly and without resentment, is part of using them effectively; the goal is a hiker who moves well, not a hiker who poles constantly.

sections.heading: Stream Crossings and Wet Footing: Poles as a Third and Fourth Leg
sections.body:
Water crossings are where poles graduate from convenience to genuine safety equipment, and also where the rules tighten. The first rule precedes technique: assess before you commit. Moving water is far stronger than it looks; a knee-deep current at a fast walking pace can take an adult's feet away, and thigh-deep fast water is a genuine drowning hazard regardless of technique or equipment. Scout up and down stream for the widest, shallowest braid, ripples usually mean shallower water than glassy smoothness, and favor a crossing that runs out onto something forgiving downstream rather than above rapids, a strainer of fallen branches, or a drop. If the water is flood-colored, carrying debris, or above your knees and pushing hard, the effective use of trekking poles is to walk them back the way you came; no crossing on a day hike is worth a swim in current.

When the crossing is reasonable, prepare deliberately. Take both hands out of the straps and keep them out: a pole wedged between bottom rocks with your wrist strapped to it can anchor you in the current, and you must be able to jettison a stuck pole instantly. Unbuckle your pack's hip belt and sternum strap so you can shed it if you go down. Consider footwear: bare feet on unknown cobbles are a poor tool, so cross in your boots or in carried water shoes. Lengthen both poles a few centimeters, since the streambed is lower than the banks, and face slightly upstream.

The technique is three points of contact, always. You have four contacts available, two feet and two poles, and the discipline is to move only one at a time: plant both poles firmly on the bottom, move one foot; re-set one pole, then the other; move the other foot. Shuffle rather than stride, keeping your feet low and feeling each placement before loading it, and lead with your feet angled slightly upstream, side-on to the current to present less area. The poles do triple duty: they prop you against the push, they probe depth and bottom quality one step ahead, and they find the holes and greased rocks before your boots do. Plant poles upstream of your line so the current pushes them into the bottom rather than sweeping them away from you. Keep your eyes on the far bank or the water surface near your next step, not on the mesmerizing flow around your legs, which wrecks balance.

The same three-points discipline handles lesser wet problems. On stepping stones, plant both poles ahead and keep them loaded as you commit each foot, and assume every stone is greased until proven otherwise. On wet logs, poles reach down to the ground on either side as outriggers; if the log is high, narrow or slick, straddle-scoot it or find another way, because a fall from a log onto rocks is a worse outcome than wet boots. Wet clay, algae-slicked slabs and polished boardwalks all reward shortened steps, lowered speed and both tips down. After any immersion, poles need the same courtesy as after rain: sections separated and dried at camp, because water trapped inside shafts corrodes aluminum, seizes twist locks, and freezes solid on cold nights, and a frozen lock the next morning is a pole stuck at the wrong length all day.
steps: Scout the crossing: choose wide, shallow, rippled water with a safe runout, and refuse fast water above the knees or any flood-swollen channel.
Remove both hands from the pole straps and unbuckle your pack's hip belt and sternum strap.
Lengthen both poles slightly, face partly upstream, and enter with feet angled side-on to the current.
Plant both poles firmly upstream of your line, then move one foot, feeling and testing the placement before loading it.
Re-set the poles one at a time, keeping three points of contact on the bottom at every moment, and shuffle rather than stride.
If a pole wedges, release it rather than fight it, and if you are pushed off balance, face downstream with feet up if swept away.
On the far bank, re-buckle your pack, drain and dry the poles when you can, and re-fit straps only once past the hazard.

sections.heading: Snow, Sand and Scree: Baskets, Braking and Soft-Ground Technique
sections.body:
Soft and sliding surfaces change what a pole plant means, because the ground itself gives way under load, and the hardware and technique both adapt. Snow comes first. Swap the small trekking baskets for wide snow baskets, eight to ten centimeters across; without them, poles spear through soft snow to the grip and give you nothing. On consolidated snow, technique is close to normal hiking with more deliberate plants; on soft snow, expect the plant to sink and settle before it holds, and time your push accordingly. Kicking steps up a snow slope, plant both poles uphill, kick two steps, re-plant; descending soft snow with plunge steps, keep both poles ahead and wide for continuous support. On traverses of firm snow, shorten the uphill pole and lengthen the downhill one, exactly as on a dirt sidehill, and understand the limits: trekking poles are not an ice axe, cannot arrest a slide on hard or icy snow, and a slope steep and firm enough to make you think about self-arrest is a slope for an axe, traction devices and the training to use them. Winter hikers should also tighten lever locks before the season, since cold makes plastics slip, and clear snow from the locks before adjusting; a pole that collapses when loaded on a snow slope is a fall generator. In deep cold, keep straps loose enough for gloves, and knock accumulated snow off baskets occasionally, since a kilogram of ice on each pole ruins the swing.

Sand and other loose dry ground, dunes, volcanic ash, deep pine duff, behaves like slow snow: plants sink, pushes smear, and wide baskets help more than you would expect. Lean into shorter steps and accept that pole propulsion is muted; the stability dividend remains, especially descending dune faces, where long poles and heels-first plunge steps make elegant, controlled descents of slopes that would otherwise be a slither.

Scree and talus deserve their own respect. Scree, the small sliding gravel of mountainsides, moves underfoot by design, and ascending it is tedious pole work: shortened poles, plants above you that will themselves slide a little, and patience with a two-steps-up-one-step-back economy; where a climbers' path zigzags, follow it rather than plowing straight up. Descending scree is, for many, the sport's guilty pleasure, the controlled skating glissade called scree-running, and poles transform it: lengthen both, keep the tips trailing wide behind you like a skier's poles, weight on your heels, knees soft, and let each step slide a boot-length before it locks, with the poles making continuous light contact for trim and the occasional firm stab to check speed. Keep your hands out of the straps, the sliding-wedge hazard again, and never scree-run above cliffs or other people, since you and a bow-wave of rocks arrive together. Talus, the larger stable-to-wobbly blocks, is the opposite problem: pole tips wedge in the gaps between rocks, so many experienced hikers collapse and stow poles for long talus fields and use their hands; if you keep them, plant deliberately on rock faces rather than into holes, and stay out of the straps. Across all soft-ground surfaces, the shared principles hold: bigger baskets when the ground swallows tips, longer poles when the surface is lower than you, straps off when a caught pole could hurt you, and plants tested before they are trusted.

sections.heading: Heavy Packs, Camp Chores and Trekking-Pole Shelters
sections.body:
The heavier the pack, the harder poles work. Extra load amplifies every argument in this guide: more mass arriving on each downhill step for the poles to share, a higher center of gravity for them to stabilize, and more total fatigue for the arms to absorb. Under a genuinely heavy pack, expect to shorten your usual settings a touch, since big loads compress posture, and expect the stability dividend to matter more than the propulsion one; a stumble under thirty kilograms is a different event from a stumble under five. Loading and unloading also change: poles make excellent props for the sit-down-and-strap-in method, and planting both poles lets you lever yourself and the pack upright from a log or the ground with your arms rather than a lurch. During breaks, two poles and a tree make a serviceable pack stand that keeps your load off wet ground.

Camp is where poles moonlight. The largest second career is the trekking-pole shelter: an entire category of tents and tarps, from simple flat tarps to sophisticated pyramid and A-frame designs, dispenses with dedicated tent poles and pitches on your trekking poles instead, saving several hundred grams from the total kit. If you go this route, check compatibility before buying either half: shelter designs specify a required pole height, commonly in the range of about 114 to 125 centimeters, sometimes achieved by lashing two poles together, and your poles must reach it, which rules out some short fixed-length models. Adjustable poles shine here, since fine-tuning pole height is how such shelters are tensioned taut. Handle the obvious caveat: a pole holding up your shelter is not available for an evening walk, and a pole bent during the day is now also a shelter problem, one more argument for aluminum's bend-not-break failure mode on remote trips.

The improvisation list runs long. A pole is a monopod for steadying binoculars or a camera, and several manufacturers sell camera mounts that thread into the grip. Two poles frame a clothesline; one pole props a bivy hood or holds a tarp door open. A pole extends your reach to retrieve a snagged bear-bag line, tests the depth of a suspect snow bridge or bog before you commit, and sweeps morning dew or spider webs from overgrown trail. In wildlife country, raised poles make you taller and more emphatic while you speak firmly and back away; they are a psychological tool, not a weapon, and no substitute for proper food storage and distance. For first aid, a pole is a ready-made splint stiffener and, lashed between two packs or jackets, part of an improvised stretcher frame; taping a few wraps of duct tape and a spare tip around the shaft costs nothing and travels well. None of these justify buying poles on their own, but together they mean the two sticks strapped to your pack are among the most multi-purpose objects you carry, and thinking of them that way, as general-purpose struts rather than single-use walking aids, is the mindset of an efficient backcountry traveler.

sections.heading: Care, Cleaning and Field Repairs: Keeping Poles Working
sections.body:
Trekking poles are simple machines that fail in predictable ways, and nearly all failures trace to moisture, grit or neglect at the joints. The single most important habit costs one minute: after any wet day, and after every trip, separate the sections completely and let them dry overnight before storing them nested. Water trapped inside shafts corrodes aluminum from the inside, delaminates nothing on carbon but seizes its hardware, breeds the white oxide crust that makes sections grind, and in winter freezes locks solid. Store poles dry, loosely assembled or apart, with lever locks open to relax their springs, somewhere that is not a hot car trunk, since heat ages plastic parts and glued grips.

Clean the joints when adjustment starts to feel gritty: pull the sections, wipe them with a dry or barely damp cloth, and let them dry. Resist the intuitive urge to lubricate; oil or silicone inside a twist-lock pole is the classic self-inflicted failure, because twist locks hold by friction and a lubricated expander will slip forever after. Lever locks tolerate a tiny drop of oil on the lever pivot only, never on the shaft surfaces the clamp grips. When a lever lock slips under load, the fix is the small tension screw or dial on the clamp: tighten it a quarter turn, close the lever, and test; the lever should snap shut with firm, deliberate pressure. When a twist lock spins without catching, the internal expander has usually unscrewed completely: pull the section out, hold the plastic expander, and turn the shaft to re-thread it a couple of turns, then re-tension gently.

Tips and baskets are consumables. The carbide stud itself lasts years, but inspect the plastic tip body for cracks and the carbide for rounding; replacement tips from the manufacturer press or screw on, with stubborn old ones softened in a mug of just-boiled water before being twisted off with pliers. Baskets thread or snap onto the collar above the tip; carry the small ones, fit them for mud, and swap to snow baskets seasonally. Grips and straps mostly need washing, since sweat salt stiffens webbing and breeds odor; mild soap and water, then a thorough dry.

Field repairs favor the prepared. A bent aluminum section can usually be straightened enough to telescope again: brace it over a knee or between two trees and bend in small increments, accepting good enough rather than perfect, since aluminum work-hardens and snaps if flexed repeatedly at one point. A cracked shaft, aluminum or carbon, is splinted like a broken bone: find a sleeve, a tent stake, a section of an old tip cover, even a stout green stick, lay it along the break, and wrap tightly with the duct tape you stored around the shaft. A failed lock can be bypassed by wrapping tape around the joint at your chosen length, turning an adjustable pole into a fixed one for the rest of the trip. Folding-pole cord failures are trailhead-only repairs; in the field, tape the joints and treat it as fixed-length. Carry spares proportional to dependence: day hikers need nothing, while a hiker whose shelter stands on their poles should carry a spare tip, a meter of duct tape, and the knowledge above. Retire a pole when a section is deeply gouged, when carbon shows cracks or fuzzy fibers, or when a straightened bend re-bends easily, because the next failure will choose its own moment, and it will not be a convenient one.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes, Trail Etiquette and When to Put the Poles Away
sections.body:
Most pole problems on the trail are technique habits, and naming them is half the cure. The leash grip: hands stuffed down through the straps from above, poles dangling, all load carried by clenched fingers; re-learn the from-below strap entry and let the webbing work. The too-long pole: shoulders up around the ears, elbows opened wide, plants landing ahead and braking every stride; drop the length until the elbow returns to ninety degrees. The decorative tap: tips flicked at the ground with no weight ever transferred, delivering the disadvantages of poles, occupied hands and swinging mass, with none of the benefits; either load the plants or stow the poles honestly. Same-side poling, right pole with right foot, twists the gait; a minute of dragging the tips restores the natural opposite swing. The forgotten adjustment: one length all day regardless of grade, which mostly means descents taken with poles too short to help; build the ten-second habit of re-setting at the top and bottom of sustained hills. And the death grip anywhere: white knuckles waste forearms and signal that straps, length or confidence need attention.

Etiquette is mostly about points and noise. Carbide tips scratch rock, and on popular routes the white scrimshaw of millions of pole strikes is now part of the visual damage the crowds bring; in heavily traveled areas, on bare slickrock, and on maintained stone staircases, fit rubber tip protectors or stow the poles. Soft trail margins mind their own wounds: planting off-trail widens paths and cuts switchback shortcuts deeper, so keep tips on the tread, and in delicate places, alpine turf, cryptobiotic desert crust, bog vegetation, keep them on rock or keep them stowed. Around people, tips are eye-level hazards for children and dogs: hold poles vertically in crowds, points down at rests, and never gesture with a pole. Give oncoming hikers the courtesy of pulling your tips in as you pass on narrow tread, and when you stop, lay poles beside the trail, not across it. In camp, capped or stowed; in shelters and huts, outside or under your bunk, since carbide and floorboards disagree.

Just as important is recognizing when poles subtract value. Scrambles where hands meet rock, ladders, chains and via ferrata sections, boulder-hopping talus, and any climbing steeper than walking all want poles collapsed and stowed on the pack, ideally before the terrain forces the decision at an awkward stance. Practice the transition until it takes under a minute: collapse, cross the shafts under compression straps or drop them tip-down in a side pocket, and go. Runners descending technical trail often carry poles mid-shaft in one hand for the same reason. And some hikers, some days, simply move better unencumbered; poles are a tool, not a uniform.

A last word on airports and buses: security rules in most countries treat trekking poles as prohibited in carry-on baggage, so check them, ship them, or buy folding poles that fit a checked duffel, and cap the tips for every form of transit. The whole discipline compresses to one sentence: poles reward the hiker who adjusts them, loads them and stows them deliberately, and they punish, mildly but daily, the hiker who merely carries them.

guides.safetyNote: Trekking poles are safety equipment only when used with judgment. Carbide tips are sharp: keep them angled down and away from people, cap them around others and in vehicles, and never run or glissade with poles in hand. Take your hands OUT of the straps for stream crossings, on terrain with fall potential where a snagged pole could wrench your arm or drag you, and anywhere a trapped pole could hold you under water. Poles do not make dangerous crossings safe: thigh-deep, fast or flood-swollen water can knock an adult down regardless of technique, and turning back is the correct choice. If you rely on poles for a balance or joint condition, ask a clinician or physical therapist about fit before depending on them.

guides.title: Uphill Walking Technique and Breathing
guides.summary: How to walk uphill efficiently and sustainably: the energetics of climbing, the gait changes that actually save effort, the rest step and pressure breathing, pacing by breath, and how technique adapts to steepness, surface, load and altitude.

sections.heading: Why Going Up Is a Skill and Not Just Effort
sections.body: Most people treat uphill walking as a matter of fitness alone: you either have the lungs for it or you do not. That is only partly true. Two walkers of identical fitness, carrying identical loads up the same slope, routinely arrive at the top with very different amounts left in the tank, and the difference is technique. Ascending is a distinct motor skill with its own rules of cadence, foot placement, posture, breathing and pacing, and it is one of the few athletic skills where a beginner can make an immediate and enormous improvement simply by being told what to do. The reason technique matters so much is that climbing is unusually expensive and unusually unforgiving of waste. On the flat, walking is close to a pendulum: the body's centre of mass rises and falls slightly with each step, and elastic recoil in the tendons plus the exchange between kinetic and potential energy recovers perhaps 60 to 70 per cent of the energy in each stride. Going uphill destroys that economy. Every step lifts the whole body mass through a real vertical distance and none of that lift comes back; it is spent as heat in the muscle when you descend. Muscles are also poor engines, converting only about 20 to 25 per cent of the chemical energy they consume into mechanical work, and the rest emerges as heat. A slope therefore turns a walker into a furnace as much as into an engine. The practical result is that on level ground a walker can absorb a great deal of sloppy technique without noticing, while on a steep hill the same sloppiness compounds every few seconds. Overstriding by twenty centimetres costs almost nothing on a pavement; repeated three thousand times on an ascent it is the difference between arriving fresh and arriving wrecked. Breathing that is adequate at sea level on the flat becomes the binding constraint within a minute of tilting the ground upward. There is also a strong psychological component, which is worth naming honestly rather than dismissing. Climbing is uncomfortable, the summit is usually out of sight, and the natural human response to discomfort is to hurry to end it. That instinct is exactly wrong. The single most common error on a hill, made by fit and unfit people alike, is starting too fast: the first ten minutes feel easy because muscle glycogen and stored oxygen mask the cost, and the debt is collected somewhere around minute twenty in the form of burning legs, ragged breathing and a forced stop. Good hill technique is therefore largely the art of doing less, more regularly: a smaller step, a slower and steadier rhythm, a breath tied to that rhythm, and an effort level chosen deliberately at the bottom rather than discovered painfully in the middle.

sections.heading: The Energetics: How Much Work a Climb Actually Costs
sections.body: The cost of climbing can be calculated rather than guessed, and the numbers are clarifying. The mechanical work of raising a mass against gravity is the mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration multiplied by the height gained. For a 75-kilogram walker carrying a 10-kilogram pack, so 85 kilograms in total, climbing 100 metres, the work is 85 times 9.81 times 100, about 83,000 joules, or roughly 20 kilocalories of pure mechanical output. Because muscle is only about 22 per cent efficient at this task, the body must actually spend around 90 kilocalories of metabolic energy for every 100 metres of ascent. A 1,000-metre mountain day therefore costs on the order of 900 kilocalories of climbing alone, before adding the cost of covering horizontal distance, the cost of descending, and basal metabolism. A useful field rule falls out of this. The metabolic cost of climbing works out at roughly 1 kilocalorie per kilogram of total weight per 100 metres of ascent. That single line explains why pack weight matters so much on hills and so little on the flat: on a 1,200-metre climb, every extra kilogram carried costs about 12 extra kilocalories, and more importantly it raises the power demanded of the legs by the same proportion for the entire duration. Rate of ascent is measured in metres of vertical gain per hour, often abbreviated VAM from the Italian velocità ascensionale media. Sustainable rates are surprisingly consistent. An unfit or heavily laden walker manages 200 to 300 metres per hour. A fit hillwalker with a day pack does 400 to 600. A well-trained mountaineer or hill runner sustains 800 to 1,000, and elite performers on mountain-running records exceed 1,800 for shorter efforts. Naismith's rule, published by the Scottish mountaineer William Naismith in 1892, encodes roughly the same thing: allow one hour per 5 kilometres of distance plus an extra hour per 600 metres of ascent. It is optimistic for heavy loads or rough ground, and most parties apply a correction factor of 1.25 to 1.5. Slope angle changes the calculation in an important way. The metabolic cost per metre of vertical gain is not constant; it is lowest on moderate gradients of roughly 15 to 25 per cent, around 9 to 14 degrees, where the legs can work close to their optimum. On gentler slopes you spend energy covering horizontal ground you do not need. On very steep ground, above about 30 degrees, cost per vertical metre climbs again because balance, hand use, high knee lift and short bracing contractions all waste energy. This is the physiological justification for switchbacks: a zigzag path is longer but often cheaper. One more number is worth carrying in the head. A rough field conversion used by hill walkers is that 100 metres of ascent costs about the same effort as one kilometre of level walking, sometimes quoted as one to one and a half kilometres depending on load and fitness. It is crude, but it makes route comparison possible on the map before you commit yourself to the ground.

sections.heading: What the Muscles Are Actually Doing
sections.body: On level ground a walker's muscles do a mixture of shortening work, lengthening braking and isometric stabilising, with the elastic tendons recycling a large fraction of the energy. Uphill, the balance shifts decisively toward concentric work, where the muscle shortens while producing force. Concentric work is metabolically expensive; the eccentric, lengthening contractions that dominate descending are cheap in energy but damaging to muscle fibres. That asymmetry is why going up leaves you breathless on the day and going down leaves you sore two days later. The prime movers of ascent are the hip extensors, above all the gluteus maximus, assisted by the hamstrings; the knee extensors, the four heads of the quadriceps; and the ankle plantar flexors, gastrocnemius and soleus. The relative contribution shifts with steepness. On gentle grades the calf does a large share, pushing the body forward and upward at the end of stance. As the slope steepens past roughly 15 degrees, hip extension takes over as the dominant contributor, and on very steep ground the glutes and quadriceps do almost all the work while the calf mainly stabilises. This has a direct coaching implication: walkers who climb by pushing off their toes will burn their calves out on steep ground, while walkers who learn to drive from the hip, standing up onto the leading leg, recruit the largest and most fatigue-resistant muscle in the body. Muscles are also strongly length-dependent. A muscle produces its greatest force near its mid-range and much less when very short or very long. When a walker takes a big step onto a high rock, the leading knee flexes deeply, the quadriceps is stretched to a mechanically poor position, and it must generate very high force through a long range. That single step can cost three or four times what two smaller steps would. It also loads the knee joint heavily: patellofemoral compression rises steeply as knee flexion increases, which is why high steps are the classic aggravator of anterior knee pain. Two further muscle groups matter more than beginners expect. The hip abductors, gluteus medius and minimus, stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance; when they fatigue, the pelvis drops on the swing side, the knee falls inward, and both efficiency and joint safety deteriorate. And the trunk muscles, including the deep abdominals and spinal erectors, work continuously to keep the torso stable against a pack and against the forward lean of climbing. A hill walker who reaches the top with an aching lower back has usually been carrying a badly packed load with a weak or fatigued trunk rather than a genuinely heavy one. None of this means that hill strength must be built on hills. Step-ups onto a knee-high box, split squats, single-leg deadlifts and loaded carries develop precisely the hip extension, single-leg stability and trunk endurance that ascending demands, and they can be done anywhere.

sections.heading: Step Length and Cadence: The Small-Step Principle
sections.body: If a walker takes only one piece of advice onto a hill, it should be this: shorten the step and keep the rhythm. Almost every efficiency problem in ascending traces back to a step that is too long for the gradient, and almost every fix begins by making it shorter. The mechanism is straightforward. Each step raises the body's centre of mass by an amount set by step length multiplied by the gradient. On a 20-degree slope, a 70-centimetre step lifts you about 25 centimetres; a 40-centimetre step lifts you about 15. The muscle does not merely do less total work per step with the shorter stride, it does that work at a far lower peak force and through a far smaller range of joint motion, which keeps it near its efficient operating length and keeps the demand within what the aerobic system can supply continuously. A long step, by contrast, produces a brief high-force effort that overshoots into anaerobic metabolism, and a series of such efforts accumulates lactate and fatigue even when the average speed is modest. The practical rule used by mountain guides is that step height should rarely exceed about a third of your own leg length, and on sustained ground should be far less: think of the height of a shallow stair, 10 to 18 centimetres, not the height of a rock ledge. As the slope steepens, the step should get shorter, not the cadence slower. On very steep ground steps of 15 to 25 centimetres are entirely normal and entirely correct, even if they feel absurdly small. Cadence should stay relatively constant. Most efficient hill walkers settle somewhere between 90 and 110 steps per minute in total, roughly 45 to 55 per leg, and hold it across changes in gradient by varying step length instead of frequency. Keeping the rhythm steady has three benefits. It maintains momentum, so less energy is spent restarting the body from stillness. It makes breathing easy to couple to the steps. And it protects against the commonest pacing error, which is to charge the steep sections and dawdle on the gentle ones, producing a jagged effort profile that is far more tiring than a smooth one at the same average speed. Beginners almost always resist this, because a short step feels slow and unimpressive. The answer is to compare arrival times rather than instantaneous speed. A walker taking small, continuous steps at a steady cadence will typically pass, by the top of a long climb, a stronger walker who is alternating bursts of long strides with rest stops, because the small-step walker is never repaying an oxygen debt. On a 600-metre ascent this difference commonly amounts to ten or fifteen minutes and a much larger difference in how much is left for the descent.

sections.heading: Foot Placement and Reading the Ground
sections.body: Uphill walking is as much a perceptual skill as a muscular one. Efficient climbers are constantly choosing where to put their feet three or four steps ahead, and the choice is being made for mechanical reasons even when it feels like instinct. The first principle is to seek the flattest available surface for each footfall, even at the cost of a slightly less direct line. A foot placed on a flat patch takes body weight through the whole sole, lets the leg push straight down the line of the bones, and requires almost no stabilising work from the ankle. A foot placed on a sloping or rounded rock must be held in position by the muscles around the ankle and the arch, which is metabolically expensive, tiring in a way that is hard to notice until the calves are burning, and far more likely to slip. The second principle is to keep the whole foot in contact where possible. Walking on the toes with the heel raised, a habit that many people fall into on steep ground, keeps the calf under continuous isometric load and turns a long climb into a calf endurance test. Where the ground is steep enough that the heel cannot reach it, that is a signal to reduce the effective angle by traversing rather than to accept toe-walking indefinitely. On grass, mud and scree the whole-foot rule also maximises friction, because friction depends on the real contact area between the boot's lugs and the surface. The third principle is to use small natural features as a staircase. Embedded rocks, tree roots, tussocks and eroded steps let you gain height on a level platform rather than on a slope. The important discipline is to use them only where the step up is small; a big pull onto a knee-high block is the single most expensive movement on any trail and is best broken into two smaller movements, or bypassed. Reading ahead also means reading the surface for what it will do under load. Freshly disturbed scree runs downhill. Wet limestone and wet tree roots are treacherous, with friction perhaps half of dry. Grass on a slope is far more slippery when dew-wet or frosted than when dry. Loose stones on hardpack behave like ball bearings. The habit to build is a continuous cycle of scanning the next few metres while you walk, then glancing further ahead during easier steps, so that you are never placing a foot somewhere you have not already looked. Walkers who look only at their boots gain safety in the next step and lose it in the next ten, because they cannot see the line that avoids the problem altogether.

sections.heading: Posture, Trunk Lean and Where the Weight Sits
sections.body: The way the torso is carried on a climb determines whether the large hip muscles can contribute and whether the lungs can be filled properly, so posture is not cosmetic advice. The body should lean forward from the ankles, not fold at the waist. The distinction matters. Leaning from the ankles keeps the trunk, pelvis and head in one line, so the centre of mass stays over the supporting foot, the hip extensors work through their strong range, and the chest and abdomen stay open for breathing. Bending at the waist, in the characteristic hunch of a tiring walker, pushes the hips backwards behind the feet, which shifts the load from the glutes onto the quadriceps and lower back, compresses the diaphragm against the abdominal contents, and reduces the volume the lungs can take. The compressed posture also drops the head, which restricts the view and worsens route choice. The amount of forward lean should roughly match the slope, in the sense that the trunk stays close to perpendicular to the ground rather than to the horizontal. On a 20-degree slope that means about 10 to 15 degrees of lean; on gentle ground, almost none. Excessive lean is as inefficient as too little: it forces the spinal muscles to hold the torso up against gravity, and it moves the weight so far forward that the toes take an unreasonable share of it. Where a pack is carried is part of posture. A load carried high and close to the spine, with its centre of mass near the walker's own, requires the least compensating lean and the least trunk muscle work. A load slung low and away from the back acts on a long lever arm and forces either a pronounced lean or continuous back-muscle effort. Hip belts should carry roughly 70 to 80 per cent of the pack weight on the iliac crests, with shoulder straps merely stabilising, because the pelvis and legs are far better structures for load bearing than the shoulders and spine. Arm carriage matters more than it seems. Hands should stay low and relaxed, swinging naturally or resting on poles. Hands held high, gripping shoulder straps up near the chest, restrict rib expansion and, over an hour, produce numb fingers as the arms sit above the heart with a static grip. Similarly, gripping poles hard rather than letting the wrist strap take the load fatigues the forearms without adding propulsion. A useful self-check every ten minutes on a climb is to run down a short mental list: is my head up and my gaze twenty metres ahead, are my shoulders down and loose, am I hinged at the ankle rather than the waist, and are my hands relaxed. Correcting posture drift early is far cheaper than trying to fix it when exhausted.

sections.heading: The Rest Step: Standing on Bone Instead of Muscle
sections.body: The rest step is the oldest and most valuable technique in mountaineering, taught in essentially the same form since the Alpine guides of the nineteenth century. It allows a walker to climb continuously for hours on ground that would otherwise force a stop every few minutes, and it works by inserting a genuine micro-rest into every single stride. The principle is skeletal loading. A straight leg supports body weight through the femur, tibia and the locked knee joint, requiring almost no muscular effort; a bent leg must be held by continuous quadriceps contraction. In ordinary walking the supporting leg is never fully straight, so the thigh muscle never gets a break. The rest step deliberately straightens and briefly locks the rear leg at the end of each step, transfers the whole body weight onto that column of bone, and pauses there. Even a pause of half a second, repeated fifty times a minute, gives the working muscle a rest fraction of a quarter or more of the total time, and lets blood flow into it. Muscle blood flow is actually occluded during a strong sustained contraction, so the pause is not merely a rest but the only moment when the muscle is being resupplied. The technique feels strange at first because it produces a deliberate, slightly mechanical rhythm rather than a flowing walk, and because the pause must be real rather than notional. It is worth practising on a moderate hill before relying on it high on a mountain, and it comes into its own exactly where it is hardest to learn: on long, monotonous, steep ground at altitude, where it is often the difference between moving slowly all day and stopping every hundred metres. Pace with the rest step is set by the length of the pause, not by the speed of the leg movement. As the ground steepens or the air thins, lengthen the pause; on easier ground, shorten it until the walk becomes continuous again.
steps: Stand with your weight fully on one leg and that leg completely straight, so the knee is locked and the skeleton, not the thigh muscle, is holding you up.
Let the other leg hang completely relaxed for a moment. Feel that it is carrying nothing at all; this is the rest, and it must be genuine.
Swing the relaxed leg forward and place the foot on the flattest spot available, taking a step far shorter than feels natural, ideally 15 to 30 centimetres of height gain.
Push down and stand up onto the new leg using the hip and thigh, straightening it fully so that the knee locks and the weight settles onto bone again.
Pause there for half a second to two seconds while the trailing leg hangs relaxed, timing the pause to your breathing.
Repeat continuously, lengthening the pause on steeper ground or at altitude and shortening it as the ground eases, so the rhythm never breaks.

sections.heading: Pressure Breathing and Rhythmic Breathing
sections.body: Breathing on a climb is not something that should be left to happen. Two deliberate techniques, rhythmic breathing and pressure breathing, do more for sustainable ascent than any amount of extra leg strength, and both are simple enough to learn in a few minutes. Rhythmic breathing means locking the breath to the steps so that the two cannot drift apart. A common pattern is one full breath cycle every two steps on moderate ground, one per step on steep or high ground, and one breath every three or four steps when moving easily. The value is partly mechanical, because the diaphragm and the trunk muscles that stabilise against each footfall interfere with each other when uncoordinated, and largely regulatory: a fixed ratio turns breathing into an accurate speedometer. If you cannot maintain your chosen ratio, you are going too fast, and the correct response is to shorten the step immediately rather than to breathe harder. Pressure breathing is a forced exhalation through pursed lips against slight resistance, making a short audible puff. It was popularised in western mountaineering literature and is used routinely on high peaks. It does several things. It raises pressure in the airways during exhalation, which helps keep small airways from collapsing and improves emptying of the lungs, so the next breath draws in more fresh air rather than re-breathing stale air from the dead space. It enforces a full, active exhalation, which is the part of the breathing cycle people neglect when tired. It slows the rate and deepens the breath, improving the fraction of each breath that reaches the alveoli. And it gives the walker a clear, repeatable act to focus on, which steadies pace. Two cautions are worth stating plainly. Pressure breathing is not hyperventilation, and deliberately over-breathing to feel better will blow off carbon dioxide, constrict cerebral vessels and cause dizziness and tingling fingers. And no breathing technique substitutes for acclimatisation or for descent when altitude illness is developing.
steps: Choose a step-to-breath ratio at the bottom of the climb: one breath per two steps for moderate ground, one per step for steep ground or thin air.
Breathe in through the nose where possible, filling the lower ribs and belly rather than only the upper chest; the abdomen should move outward.
Exhale through pursed lips, as if blowing out a candle a metre away, making a short forceful puff that empties the lungs more completely than a passive breath.
Keep the exhalation slightly longer than the inhalation, roughly a two-count out to a one-count in, and never let the exhale become passive.
Hold the ratio constant as the ground changes, adjusting step length instead of breathing rate, so that the breath sets the pace.
If you cannot hold the ratio for more than a minute, stop increasing effort, shorten your step, and if necessary reduce your rate of ascent rather than pushing on.

sections.heading: What Breathing Is Actually For, and Why It Feels Hard
sections.body: It is worth understanding what the breathlessness of a climb actually signals, because the everyday assumption is wrong and the wrong assumption leads to bad pacing. Most people believe they breathe harder because their body is short of oxygen. In a healthy person at low altitude that is not the main driver. Arterial blood is roughly 97 per cent saturated with oxygen at rest and stays close to that even during hard exercise; the lungs are rarely the limiting organ. The dominant stimulus to breathe is carbon dioxide, detected by chemoreceptors in the medulla of the brainstem, with additional drive from acidity as lactate accumulates and from signals arising in the working muscles themselves. The practical consequence is that breathlessness on a hill is a report on how much metabolic waste you are producing, not a warning that you are running out of air. Slowing the legs slows carbon dioxide production and the breathing settles within thirty to sixty seconds. Breathing harder without slowing does very little, because you were never oxygen-limited in the first place. The mechanics of moving air also matter. A resting adult breathes about 12 to 16 times a minute, moving roughly half a litre per breath, so about 6 to 8 litres per minute. During hard hill walking that can rise to 60 to 100 litres per minute, and in trained athletes at maximum effort past 150. Crucially, only part of each breath reaches the gas-exchanging alveoli; roughly 150 millilitres stays in the trachea and bronchi, the anatomical dead space, and takes no part in exchange. This is the arithmetic behind the advice to breathe deeply rather than rapidly. Twenty breaths of 1 litre delivers 17 litres of fresh air to the alveoli each minute; forty breaths of half a litre, the same total volume, delivers only 14. Shallow panting is measurably less effective at the same effort. The diaphragm does about 70 per cent of the work of quiet breathing, and it is a fatigue-resistant muscle, but on a steep climb it competes with the abdominal and trunk muscles that are stabilising the torso against the pack and the stride. That competition is why a hunched posture, a tight hip belt worn too high over the lower ribs, or a chest strap fastened too tightly can each make breathing feel disproportionately hard. There is one more feedback worth knowing. Breathing costs energy itself; at high ventilation rates the respiratory muscles may consume 10 to 15 per cent of total oxygen uptake, and there is evidence that when they fatigue, reflexes divert blood flow away from the legs to protect them. This is a concrete reason to treat breathing as something to manage from the start of a climb rather than something to fix once it has gone ragged.

sections.heading: Pacing: Choosing an Effort You Can Hold for Hours
sections.body: Pacing is the master variable of hill walking, and it is decided in the first five minutes. The goal is to select an intensity that can be sustained for the whole ascent with no forced stops, which in physiological terms means staying at or just below the first ventilatory threshold, the point at which breathing first becomes disproportionate to effort. Three field tests identify that point without any equipment. The talk test is the most reliable: you should be able to speak a full sentence, not a single word and not a paragraph, without gasping. If you can only manage two or three words, you are above threshold and are accumulating a debt that will be collected later. If you can hold an unbroken conversation, you are probably below your best sustainable pace and could go a little harder if the day is long but the climb is short. The second test is nasal breathing: many walkers can breathe entirely through the nose at a sustainable pace and must open the mouth above it. The third is the breath ratio: if the step-to-breath pattern you chose at the bottom has silently doubled its frequency, your pace has drifted upward. Heart rate is a useful but slower guide. For a sustainable multi-hour ascent, most people sit around 70 to 80 per cent of maximum heart rate, which is roughly 60 to 70 per cent of heart rate reserve. Heart rate lags effort by a minute or two and drifts upward through a long day at constant effort, a phenomenon called cardiac drift caused mainly by dehydration and rising core temperature, so it should be read as a trend rather than a switch. The deepest pacing error is to attack the steep sections. The correct instinct is exactly inverted: go slower where it is steeper, keeping effort constant rather than speed constant. A steady effort up a variable hill means a visibly variable speed, and that is right. Warming up matters more on hills than on the flat, because the first ten minutes of any climb come before the cardiovascular and metabolic systems have fully adjusted. Starting deliberately easy for the first ten to fifteen minutes, at what feels almost embarrassingly slow, allows heart rate, blood flow redistribution and fat metabolism to come up to speed, and it very reliably produces a faster overall time than starting hard. Regular short stops of one to two minutes every 45 to 60 minutes, taken to drink and adjust clothing before you feel you need them, are more effective than long stops taken when you are exhausted, which cool the muscles and stiffen them. Pacing in a group needs one further rule: the party moves at the speed of its slowest member, and the slowest member should walk at or near the front. Placing them at the back means they are permanently chasing, working above their sustainable threshold, and arriving at each stop with no rest at all while everyone ahead has already recovered.

sections.heading: Trekking Poles: What They Do and How to Use Them
sections.body: Poles change the mechanics of ascent, and the evidence for their benefits is reasonably good, though it is often overstated in advertising. What poles reliably do is transfer some of the work from the legs to the arms and trunk, improve balance on uneven ground, and reduce the peak forces through the knee. Studies of pole use on ascents generally find they take something in the region of 5 to 15 per cent of the load off the lower limbs. What they usually do not do is reduce total energy consumption; several studies find oxygen uptake at a given speed is unchanged or slightly higher with poles, because the arms are now working too. The gain is distribution of fatigue rather than less of it, and reduced joint loading, which is a real benefit over a long day and over a lifetime of hills. Length is the first thing to get right, and it must change with terrain. On the flat, the pole should put the elbow at roughly 90 degrees when the tip is on the ground beside the foot; for most people that is around 120 to 130 centimetres. For ascending, shorten them by 5 to 15 centimetres, because the ground ahead of you is higher than the ground under you and a long pole forces the arm up into a weak, tiring position. For descending, lengthen by a similar amount. Walkers who set their poles once in the car park and never change them are getting a fraction of the benefit. The wrist strap does the work, not the grip. The correct method is to bring the hand up through the loop from below and then close it around the handle so that the strap runs across the palm; body weight then presses down through the strap into the pole, and the fingers need only guide it. A tight fist around the handle fatigues the forearms within an hour and produces the familiar sausage fingers of long days out. The rhythm is normally opposite arm to opposite leg, which mirrors natural walking and stabilises the pelvis. On very steep ground many walkers switch to double-poling, planting both poles together and pulling on both while taking one or two steps, which is powerful but tiring and best reserved for short pitches. Plant the tips just ahead of the leading foot, not far out in front, and push down and back rather than pulling forward; a pole planted too far ahead becomes a brake. Poles have real drawbacks. They occupy the hands, which is dangerous on ground where you may need them for balance on rock, and they can catch in vegetation or between rocks. On scrambling terrain they should be stowed before the ground demands hands, not during.

sections.heading: Carrying a Load Uphill
sections.body: Weight is the cruellest variable on a climb, because its cost is proportional and unrelenting. Carrying an extra 5 kilograms on a 1,000-metre ascent adds roughly 50 kilocalories of climbing work and, more importantly, raises the power your legs must produce by about 6 per cent for every minute of the climb. Since most walkers are already near their sustainable ceiling, that extra 6 per cent usually translates into a slower pace rather than a harder effort. The commonly quoted guidance is that a pack should not exceed about 20 per cent of body weight for comfortable day walking, and up to 25 or at most 30 per cent for experienced walkers on multi-day trips. Military and load-carriage research broadly supports these figures: metabolic cost rises roughly in proportion to load up to about 30 per cent of body weight, then rises faster than proportionally as gait itself begins to deteriorate. Above roughly a third of body weight, stride shortens involuntarily, trunk lean increases, and both injury risk and energy cost climb sharply. How the load is packed matters nearly as much as how much it weighs. The heaviest items should sit close to the spine and roughly between the shoulder blades for hill walking, keeping the combined centre of mass near the walker's own and minimising the compensating lean. Carrying the same mass low and away from the back, in a bulging bottom pocket or a sleeping mat strapped far out, produces a longer lever arm and measurably more trunk work. On very steep or technical ground some walkers deliberately carry the weight slightly lower to lower the centre of gravity for balance, accepting a small efficiency penalty for stability, which is a reasonable trade. Fitting a pack is a sequence, not a single adjustment. Loosen everything, load the pack, put it on, settle the hip belt on the iliac crests with the padding centred on the bone, tighten the belt, then snug the shoulder straps until they contact the shoulders without lifting the load off the hips, then adjust the load-lifter straps at the top to roughly 45 degrees, and finally fasten the sternum strap loosely, about 2 to 3 centimetres below the collarbone, only to keep the shoulder straps from splaying. A sternum strap pulled tight is a common and self-inflicted cause of breathlessness. Weight on the feet is disproportionately expensive. Research on load carriage consistently finds that mass carried on the foot costs roughly four to six times as much energy per kilogram as the same mass in a pack, because it must be accelerated and decelerated with every stride. A pair of boots 400 grams heavier per foot than necessary can cost as much as 2 to 5 kilograms in the pack. This is the strongest single argument for wearing the lightest footwear that gives adequate support and grip for the ground you will actually meet.

sections.heading: Adapting to Steepness: Traverses, Switchbacks and Very Steep Ground
sections.body: Technique should change as the gradient changes, and knowing which technique belongs to which angle saves a great deal of effort and some danger. On gentle ground up to about 10 degrees, ordinary walking works with only minor adjustments: a slightly shorter step, a modest forward lean from the ankle, and attention to rhythm. Between roughly 10 and 25 degrees, which covers the majority of maintained mountain paths, the small-step principle and rhythmic breathing become the dominant tools, and the rest step starts to pay off on the longer pitches. Above about 25 to 30 degrees, direct ascent becomes inefficient and often unpleasant, and the answer is to reduce the effective angle rather than to fight it. Traversing does exactly that. Walking diagonally across a slope rather than straight up it converts a steep line into a shallower one at the cost of extra distance. A path taken at 45 degrees to the fall line halves the effective gradient. Switchbacks, the zigzags built into engineered mountain trails, are the formalised version, and their purpose is as much erosion control as walker comfort: a direct line channels water and destroys the hillside. Cutting a switchback is both a technique error and an act of vandalism, since it starts the gully that eventually washes the path away. On steep ground the feet need to change too. The duck walk, splaying the toes outward by 30 to 45 degrees, lets the ankle reach the ground when it could not otherwise, keeps the heel down, and relieves the calf; it is awkward on the flat and invaluable on a steep grassy or earth slope. On firmer steep ground, edging the boot sideways into the slope and moving across it in a herringbone pattern gives more contact and better purchase. Where hands become necessary, the rule is three points of contact and deliberate testing of each hold before weighting it. The turn at the end of a traverse is a small technique with real consequences, because it is a common place to slip. Turn into the slope, not away from it, so that if you lose balance you fall toward the hillside rather than out into space, and plant the uphill pole or hand before rotating the feet. Finally, know when the technique stops applying. Ground steeper than roughly 40 to 45 degrees, or any ground where a slip would carry you into a drop, is no longer walking terrain but scrambling or climbing terrain, with different equipment, different judgement and different consequences. The most important skill on steepening ground is recognising the transition early, while retreat is still easy. A useful discipline is to read gradient from the map before meeting it. On a 1:25,000 map with 10 metre contours, contours 4 millimetres apart represent a 10 per cent slope, and contours touching represent ground steep enough to require hands. Knowing which technique a section will demand before you reach it is worth more than any amount of improvisation on the spot.

sections.heading: Surfaces: Scree, Snow, Mud, Grass, Rock and Steps
sections.body: The same slope demands different technique depending on what it is made of, and matching technique to surface is largely a matter of understanding how each one fails under a foot. Loose scree and gravel move when pushed backwards, so power applied along the slope simply accelerates the stones. The answer is to place the foot flat, weight it vertically and gently, and avoid any push-off; look for larger embedded stones and the compacted edges of the scree run, which are usually more stable, and step on the uphill side of any rock rather than the downhill side where it may roll. Kick a small platform if the scree is fine enough to hold one. Snow rewards a positive kick. Kick-stepping means driving the toe of the boot horizontally into the slope to cut a small ledge, then standing on it, and it works because compressed snow is far stronger than undisturbed snow. On harder snow the step must be more forceful and the ledge smaller, and there comes a point, when the boot no longer bites, at which crampons and an ice axe are not optional extras but the minimum requirement; a slip on hard snow accelerates alarmingly and self-arrest is a trained skill, not an instinct. Mud and wet grass fail by shearing, so the priority is maximising contact and avoiding lateral force. Place the whole sole down, keep the step short, and prefer tussocks, exposed roots and the vegetated margins of a path to its polished centre. On wet grass in particular, the friction available may be less than half that of dry grass, and a slope that is a comfortable walk dry can be genuinely dangerous wet. Rock rewards trust in friction. On dry rough rock such as gritstone or granite, a boot with a clean sole will hold at far steeper angles than most people expect, provided the weight is directly over the foot; leaning into the slope reduces the normal force and makes a slip more likely, which is why standing upright on steep rock feels wrong and is correct. Wet limestone, serpentine and lichen-covered rock are the notable exceptions and should be treated as slippery until proven otherwise. Constructed steps, common on popular paths and on stairways, are efficient but unforgiving, because they impose their own step height rather than letting you choose it. Where they are high, use the edge as a platform for a half step where possible, alternate the leading leg to spread the load, and if a flight is long, treat it exactly like a steep pitch: shorten what you can, slow the cadence slightly, and hold the breathing ratio.

sections.heading: Climbing at Altitude: Thinner Air and Slower Everything
sections.body: Above roughly 1,500 metres the air itself becomes a limiting factor, and above 2,500 metres it reshapes technique entirely. The composition of air does not change with height; it remains about 21 per cent oxygen. What falls is total pressure, and therefore the partial pressure of oxygen. At sea level atmospheric pressure is about 1,013 hectopascals; at 3,000 metres it is around 700, at 5,500 metres roughly half of sea level, and on the summit of Everest at 8,849 metres about a third. Because oxygen loading in the lungs depends on partial pressure, the driving pressure for oxygen uptake falls in proportion. The performance consequence is predictable and steep. Maximum aerobic capacity falls by roughly 6 to 10 per cent for every 1,000 metres above about 1,500 metres in unacclimatised people. At 3,000 metres a walker may have lost a fifth of their capacity, and at 5,000 metres closer to a third to a half. Rates of ascent that felt easy at home become impossible, and the correct response is not to try harder but to accept a slower pace, shorter steps and a breathing ratio of one full cycle per step or even per half step. The body responds immediately with hyperventilation, driven by the carotid bodies sensing low oxygen. This helps, but blowing off carbon dioxide makes the blood alkaline, which paradoxically restrains the very breathing that is helping; the kidneys correct this over one to several days by excreting bicarbonate, which is a large part of what acclimatisation means. Other adaptations follow over days to weeks: increased red cell production driven by erythropoietin, higher capillary density, and changes in muscle metabolism. Altitude illness is the practical hazard. Acute mountain sickness typically appears 6 to 12 hours after arriving above about 2,500 metres and presents as headache with nausea, poor appetite, tiredness and disturbed sleep. It is common, affecting perhaps a quarter of people at 3,000 metres, and usually settles with a rest day. The two dangerous forms are high-altitude pulmonary oedema, signalled by breathlessness at rest, a dry then productive cough and marked drop in performance, and high-altitude cerebral oedema, signalled by confusion and an unsteady, drunken gait. Both are life-threatening and the treatment for both is immediate descent, ideally 500 to 1,000 metres, without waiting for morning. The classic prevention rules remain sound: above 3,000 metres, increase sleeping altitude by no more than 300 to 500 metres per night, take a rest day every 3 to 4 days or every 1,000 metres, and climb high but sleep low. Drink enough that urine stays pale, since dehydration is accelerated by dry air and heavy breathing, and avoid alcohol and sedatives on ascent days.

sections.heading: What Goes Wrong, and What to Do About It
sections.body: Most hill days that go badly go badly in one of a small number of recognisable ways, and nearly all of them are recoverable if caught early. Blowing the pace is the commonest. The signs are ragged breathing that will not settle within a minute of easing off, burning quadriceps, and an urge to stop every few minutes. The fix is immediate and unglamorous: cut the step length in half, restore the breathing ratio, and hold that for five to ten minutes. Do not stop and rest; stopping cools the muscles and the debt is repaid more slowly than by simply walking slower. Once breathing is under control, increase pace only enough to pass the talk test. Overheating is the second. Climbing generates heat at three or four times resting rate, and a walker in a windproof layer on a still day can build core temperature quickly. Sweat-soaked base layers then become a hypothermia risk the moment you stop or reach a windy ridge. The discipline is to start cold, deliberately underdressed for the first few minutes, ventilate early by opening pit zips and removing a layer before you are wet rather than after, and to put an insulating layer on within a minute of stopping. Cramp usually strikes the calf or the hamstring late in a climb. Its causes are still genuinely debated: the older explanation of salt and fluid depletion has been challenged by evidence pointing to neuromuscular fatigue and altered reflex control, and the honest position is that both probably contribute. In practice, gentle sustained stretching of the affected muscle relieves an attack within a minute or two, and prevention centres on pacing, adequate fluid with some sodium on long hot days, and not making sudden jumps in training volume. Knee pain on ascent, felt at the front of the knee, is usually a sign of repeated high steps and deep knee flexion under load. Shortening the step, using poles and choosing lines with smaller individual rises usually settles it. Pain on the outside of the knee, more often on descent, suggests iliotibial band irritation and responds to shorter steps and reduced pack weight. Finally, and most importantly, know the signals that mean turn around rather than adjust: chest pain or pressure, particularly with sweating or nausea; confusion, slurred speech or a staggering gait; breathlessness at rest that does not settle; a member of the party who has stopped sweating and is hot and confused; deteriorating weather with a long exposed section still to come; or simply arriving at a fixed turnaround time short of the summit. A turnaround time agreed at the bottom, and honoured without negotiation, is the single most effective safety technique in hill walking, and it works precisely because it is decided before fatigue and summit fever have had a chance to distort judgement.

guides.safetyNote: Steep ground, snow, loose rock and altitude carry real risk of injury and death. Descend immediately for confusion, staggering, breathlessness at rest or chest pain, and treat ground where a slip would carry you into a drop as climbing terrain requiring proper equipment and training rather than walking terrain.

guides.title: Side Hilling and Traversing Slopes
guides.summary: How to move across a slope rather than up or down it: the physics that makes traversing uniquely tiring and dangerous, the footwork and body position that make it survivable, and how to choose a line, read a surface and retreat when the ground turns against you.

sections.heading: What Side Hilling Is and Why It Punishes You
sections.body:
Side hilling, also called traversing or contouring, means moving horizontally across a slope instead of climbing straight up it or descending straight down. On a map it looks like the efficient choice: you follow a contour line, you gain no height, you lose none, and the distance is often shorter than the alternative. In practice it is one of the most tiring, most awkward and most quietly dangerous things a person on foot can do, and experienced mountain travellers will frequently accept several hundred metres of unnecessary climbing to avoid a long traverse.

The reason is that the human body is built for locomotion on level ground and adapts reasonably well to going up or down, but not to being tilted sideways. Walking uphill and downhill uses the muscles and joints roughly symmetrically: both legs do the same job in turn. On a traverse they do completely different jobs. The uphill leg is short-stepping onto ground above you, working its hip abductors and its inner ankle; the downhill leg is reaching down and out, taking most of the load, and holding your whole mass against a constant sideways pull. Your ankles are forced into sustained inversion on one side and eversion on the other, positions they can hold briefly but not for hours. Your pelvis is permanently out of level, which twists the spine. If you carry a pack, its mass sits off to one side of your base of support and levers you outward.

The result is a set of characteristic complaints that anyone who has crossed a long steep hillside will recognise: the outside of the downhill ankle burning, the arch of the uphill foot cramping, the hip flexor on the downhill side seizing, and a peculiar grinding tiredness that does not match the distance covered. The energy cost is real and measurable: studies of load carriage and gradient walking generally find that traversing steep ground costs substantially more than the horizontal distance alone would suggest, though the precise multiplier depends heavily on surface and angle and no single figure should be trusted.

The danger is separate from the effort, and it is the more important half. On a traverse, a slip does not simply drop you onto the ground; it drops you onto a surface that is already falling away, and you continue to travel. A stumble while walking uphill usually ends with your hands on the slope in front of your face. The same stumble on a traverse can start a slide that accelerates, and on hard snow, wet grass or loose scree above a drop, a slide that starts is very difficult to stop. Almost every experienced party has a story about a traverse that seemed trivial until somebody's foot went. Treating side hilling with the respect it deserves, and knowing when to refuse it, is a core skill of moving through mountain and hill country.

sections.heading: The Physics of a Slope
sections.body:
Everything about slope travel follows from resolving the force of gravity into two components. Imagine standing on a plane tilted at angle theta from horizontal. Your weight, W, which is your mass multiplied by gravitational acceleration of about 9.81 metres per second squared, points straight down. That force splits into a component pressing you into the slope, equal to W times the cosine of theta, and a component pulling you along the slope surface, equal to W times the sine of theta. The first component is what generates friction and holds you in place; the second is what tries to take you downhill.

Whether you stay put depends on friction. The maximum friction force available is the normal force multiplied by the coefficient of static friction, mu, a number describing how well the two surfaces grip each other. So you remain stable as long as W sine theta is less than mu times W cosine theta. The weight cancels out entirely, which is a genuinely important result: on a simple rigid slope, whether you slip does not depend on how heavy you are. Dividing through gives the condition that tangent theta must be less than mu. The angle at which tangent theta exactly equals mu is called the friction angle, or in the case of loose granular material the angle of repose.

Typical values give a feel for the numbers. Good rubber on dry rough rock might reach a coefficient around 0.8 or higher, corresponding to a friction angle near 39 degrees or more, which is why confident scrambling on dry rock at moderate angles feels secure. Rubber on wet smooth rock may fall to 0.3, a friction angle of about 17 degrees. Boot soles on wet flattened grass can be lower still, sometimes approaching 0.2, meaning an 11-degree slope is genuinely slippery. Dry scree and sand settle at an angle of repose usually between 30 and 37 degrees, which is why loose slopes so often present that same characteristic steepness. Hard névé or ice may offer a coefficient of 0.05 to 0.1 for a smooth boot sole, meaning almost any angle at all is unstable without crampons.

Two refinements matter in practice. First, the weight cancellation only holds for a rigid surface; on loose or soft ground a heavier person with a heavy pack does sink deeper and does displace more material, so mass reappears indirectly. Second, once you are moving, the coefficient of kinetic friction is lower than the static one, sometimes considerably. This is the physical reason a slip is so hard to arrest: the moment you start sliding, the grip available to you drops, and the accelerating force stays the same. Stopping a slide therefore requires generating force by some other means, digging in, rather than hoping friction will recover.

sections.heading: Reading Slope Angle Before You Commit
sections.body:
People are consistently bad at estimating slope angle by eye, and the error runs in a predictable direction: almost everyone overestimates. A slope that a novice calls forty-five degrees is commonly twenty-five to thirty. This matters because the thresholds that govern real decisions sit in narrow bands. Avalanche release on snow is concentrated between roughly 30 and 45 degrees, with the peak around 35 to 40. Loose scree sits near 35. Walking without hands becomes difficult above roughly 30 to 35 degrees on most surfaces. Confusing thirty for forty-five means every one of those judgements is wrong.

Several methods give a real number. The simplest is a clinometer, which is either a standalone instrument, a feature on many compasses, or an application on a phone using the internal accelerometer. Sight along the slope surface, hold the instrument in the plane of the fall line, and read the angle. Accuracy depends on picking a representative section rather than a local bulge, and on holding the instrument along the true steepest line rather than obliquely, which always reads shallower than reality.

A map gives you the angle in advance, which is far more useful, because it lets you plan rather than react. Slope angle is derived from contour spacing. If the contour interval is 10 metres and adjacent contours are 20 metres apart on the ground, the gradient is 10 over 20, or 0.5, and the angle is the arctangent of 0.5, about 27 degrees. To convert map distance to ground distance, measure the separation in millimetres and multiply by the scale: on a 1:25,000 map, 1 millimetre is 25 metres, so contours 0.8 millimetres apart represent 20 metres. A useful rule of thumb for 1:25,000 maps with 10-metre intervals is that contours about 1 millimetre apart indicate roughly 22 degrees, half a millimetre roughly 39 degrees, and touching contours mean cliff.

The pole-and-string method needs no instrument. Hold a trekking pole vertically with a weighted cord hanging from the top, and a second pole laid against the slope surface; the angle between the cord and the second pole is the slope angle, and 45 degrees is easy to identify because the geometry forms an isosceles triangle. Alternatively, plant one pole vertically in the snow or ground and touch the slope surface with a second pole held horizontally: if the horizontal pole touches the slope at the midpoint of the vertical pole, the angle is about 27 degrees; at a quarter of the way up, about 14; comparisons like this are crude but they anchor the eye.

Whatever method you use, remember that a slope is rarely uniform. The angle that matters is the steepest section you will actually cross, and the consequence that matters is what lies below it.

sections.heading: The Ankle Problem and What Traversing Does to the Body
sections.body:
The single most limiting factor on a long traverse is usually the ankle, and understanding why explains most of the technique that follows. The ankle joint proper, the talocrural joint, is essentially a hinge that allows the foot to point up and down, dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, through roughly 20 degrees up and 50 degrees down. Sideways movement, tilting the sole inward or outward, happens mostly at the subtalar joint below it, and the available range is far smaller: inversion, tilting the sole inward, reaches around 20 to 30 degrees, and eversion, tilting it outward, only around 5 to 15 degrees. Eversion is the more restricted direction by a wide margin.

On a traverse, the downhill foot must evert to keep its sole in contact with a surface that slopes away, while the uphill foot must invert. Because eversion has so little range, the downhill ankle runs out of movement first, and beyond that point the foot simply cannot lie flat and only the outside edge of the sole is loaded. This is the mechanical reason the downhill ankle hurts, and the reason most traverse injuries are on the downhill side. It also explains why reversing direction, turning round and traversing back the other way for a while, gives such immediate relief: the two ankles swap roles.

The knee is affected next. With the foot fixed and the pelvis tilted, the downhill knee is pushed into valgus, meaning it drifts inward relative to the hip and ankle, loading the medial structures and the iliotibial band on the outside of the thigh. Sustained for hours this produces the lateral knee pain many hillwalkers know. The hip abductors, principally gluteus medius, work continuously on the uphill side to stop the pelvis dropping, and their fatigue is what eventually produces a wobbling, unstable gait that no amount of concentration corrects.

Two further consequences deserve naming. First, the leg-length discrepancy is functional rather than real: on a 30-degree slope with feet a metre apart across the fall line, the uphill foot sits roughly 58 centimetres higher than the downhill one, which the body must absorb through hip, knee and ankle. Second, proprioception, your sense of where your limbs are, is calibrated for level ground, and on a sustained tilt it drifts, which is why people emerging from a long traverse often feel that flat ground is sloping the other way.

The practical upshot is that traversing is a time-limited activity. Technique buys you hours, not immunity. Plan traverses to be as short as circumstances allow, alternate direction where the terrain permits, and treat the onset of ankle burn or abductor fatigue as a signal to change something rather than a discomfort to push through, because a fatigued abductor is precisely what fails at the moment you need it.

sections.heading: Footwear, Soles and Edging
sections.body:
Footwear matters more on a traverse than on any other kind of walking, because a traverse loads the boot in the direction it is weakest. Three properties decide performance: sole stiffness, edge definition and upper support.

Sole stiffness governs whether you can edge at all. Edging means standing on a narrow strip of sole, usually the inside edge of the uphill boot or the outside edge of the downhill one, pressed into the slope so that the boot's own rigidity holds you rather than friction across the whole sole. A stiff sole transmits your weight to that narrow strip and holds a small step. A soft, flexible sole simply folds, the foot rolls, and the edge collapses.
